title: Filosofia
blurb: Grandes perguntas, ética, a mente, maneiras de viver e bons argumentos.

cards.title: O que é a filosofia
cards.text: Filosofia significa "amor à sabedoria". Ela faz perguntas que a ciência não consegue resolver só com experimentos: o que é real, o que podemos saber, como devemos viver?

deep.x: The word comes from Greek: **philo** (love) and **sophia** (wisdom). Philosophy deals with questions where gathering more facts isn't enough on its own. You also have to think hard about concepts, assumptions and arguments.

Many sciences began as philosophy. Physics was once "natural philosophy", and Isaac Newton's great book of 1687 is called *Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy*. Psychology split off only in the late 1800s. When a question becomes answerable by experiment, it tends to leave home and become its own science.
What philosophers actually do

x: Clarify concepts: what do we mean by "fair", "cause" or "person"?
Find hidden assumptions behind everyday beliefs
Build arguments and test them against counterexamples
Ask what follows if a view is true, including awkward consequences

deep.x: The two often work together. Debates about brain death, artificial intelligence or climate justice need both scientific facts and careful thinking about values.
A doctorate in almost any subject, from chemistry to economics, is called a PhD: Doctor of Philosophy, a fossil of the time when all serious study was philosophy.
Philosophy starts where facts alone stop settling the question.

cards.title: Antes de Sócrates
cards.text: Os primeiros filósofos gregos buscaram explicações naturais em vez de mitos. Tales disse que tudo era água; Heráclito, que tudo flui; Demócrito imaginou os átomos.

deep.x: Around 600 BCE, in Greek cities on the coast of what is now Turkey, a few thinkers tried something new. Instead of explaining storms and earthquakes by the moods of gods, they looked for natural causes and general principles. Historians call them the **Presocratics**.
Big ideas, little evidence

x: **Thales** said everything is made of water. Wrong, but a bold attempt to find one underlying stuff.
**Anaximander** proposed a boundless, undefined substance and guessed that humans came from fish-like creatures.
**Heraclitus** stressed constant change: you can't step into the same river twice.
**Parmenides** argued the opposite: real change is impossible, and our senses mislead us.
**Democritus** and his teacher Leucippus imagined tiny, uncuttable pieces moving in empty space: *atomos* means "uncuttable".

deep.x: What mattered was less the answers than the method. They gave reasons, criticised each other and expected rivals to argue back. That habit of open disagreement is the real birth of philosophy and, later, of science.
Thales is said to have predicted a solar eclipse in 585 BCE. Historians debate whether he really could, but the story shows how early Greeks linked thinking with nature.
The first philosophers swapped "the gods did it" for "what is it made of, and why?"

cards.title: Sócrates
cards.text: Sócrates (c. 470–399 a.C.) não escreveu nada. Ele questionava as pessoas nas ruas de Atenas até que elas vissem as falhas no que achavam que sabiam. Atenas o condenou à morte.

deep.x: Socrates (c. 470–399 BCE) was a stonemason's son who served as a soldier and spent his days talking in the agora, Athens' public square. He wrote nothing. We know him mainly through his student Plato, the historian Xenophon and a mocking comedy by Aristophanes, *The Clouds*, and their portraits don't always agree.

His habit was to ask people who claimed expertise, such as generals, politicians and poets, to define things like courage or justice. Each definition met a counterexample, until the expert admitted confusion. Young Athenians loved watching; the experts did not.
The trial

In 399 BCE he was charged with impiety and with corrupting the young. A jury of about 500 citizens convicted him, by roughly 280 votes to 220. Athens had just lived through war defeat and a brutal oligarchy, and some of Socrates' former companions had been involved, which probably counted against him.
He refused to stop philosophising to save himself and turned down a chance to escape. He drank hemlock, a poison, in prison, talking philosophy with friends to the end.

deep.w: Socrates was a lone hero against a backward city
deep.r: Athens was a democracy, and his trial raises a hard question still debated: can a democracy wrongly silence a critic?

deep.x: Socrates showed that a question asked honestly can be more dangerous than any weapon.

cards.title: "Só sei que nada sei"

items.r: "O que me mostraria que estou errado?"

cards.text: A sabedoria de Sócrates era conhecer os limites do próprio conhecimento. "Uma vida sem exame não vale a pena ser vivida" é sua frase mais conhecida, da *Apologia* de Platão.

deep.x: A friend of Socrates asked the oracle at Delphi whether anyone was wiser than Socrates. The answer was no. Puzzled, Socrates questioned people with a reputation for wisdom and found they believed they knew things they did not. He concluded he was wiser only in one small way: he didn't think he knew what he didn't know.

deep.w: Socrates said "I know that I know nothing"
deep.r: That exact line isn't in Plato; it's a later summary of his claim not to think he knows what he doesn't

deep.x: The examined life

At his trial, as told in Plato's *Apology*, Socrates said he'd rather die than stop questioning, because a life without self-examination isn't worth living for a human being. He meant testing your beliefs about how to live, not just collecting facts.
Why it still matters

x: Admitting ignorance is the first step to learning anything
Psychologists describe a related bias: people with little skill in an area often overrate their ability
Good scientists, doctors and judges build doubt into their methods

deep.x: Knowing the edges of your knowledge is itself a kind of knowledge.

cards.title: A caverna de Platão
cards.text: Platão imaginou prisioneiros acorrentados em uma caverna que só veem sombras na parede e as tomam pela realidade. A filosofia é a dolorosa subida até a luz do Sol.

deep.x: Plato (c. 428–348 BCE) tells the story in Book VII of the *Republic*. Prisoners have been chained since childhood facing a cave wall. Behind them a fire burns, and people carry objects past it, casting shadows. The prisoners name the shadows and compete to predict them. For them, shadows are all there is.

items: The Sun: the Form of the Good

deep.x: The climb

One prisoner is freed. Turning to the fire hurts his eyes; he wants to go back to the comfortable shadows. Dragged up into daylight, he is dazzled, and only slowly can he look at reflections, then real things, then the Sun itself.

When he returns to free the others, his eyes, now used to light, stumble in the dark. The prisoners laugh at him and say the journey ruined his sight. Plato adds that they would kill anyone who tried to free them, a clear nod to Socrates' fate.
Readings today

x: Education as turning the whole person, not pouring facts into an empty head
A warning about mistaking images, propaganda or social media feeds for reality
Critics say it is elitist: who decides who has "seen the light"?

deep.x: Films such as *The Matrix* (1999) and *The Truman Show* (1998) are often read as modern retellings of the cave.
Real learning is uncomfortable, because it means turning away from what is familiar.

cards.title: As Formas de Platão
cards.text: Platão acreditava que, por trás das coisas que mudam, existem Formas perfeitas e eternas: há muitos círculos, mas cada um é uma cópia imperfeita do Círculo perfeito que compreendemos pela razão.

deep.x: Draw a circle as carefully as you can. Under a magnifying glass it's wobbly. No physical circle is perfect, yet you know exactly what a perfect circle is and can prove facts about it. Plato asked: where does that knowledge come from?

His answer was the **Forms**: perfect, unchanging patterns that exist beyond the physical world. Things we see "participate in" or copy them. A beautiful face, sunset and melody are beautiful because they share in the Form of Beauty.
Why he believed it

x: Mathematics seems to be about perfect objects we never meet in the world
We judge things as more or less equal or just, which seems to need a standard
Plato thought true knowledge must be of something that doesn't change

deep.x: The objections

Plato himself raised a famous problem in his dialogue *Parmenides*. If big things share a Form of Bigness, then the big things and the Form together seem to need another Form to explain what they share, and so on forever. Aristotle called this the "third man" argument. He also asked how a Form outside space and time could cause anything here.
Mathematicians still argue about "Platonism": the view that numbers and shapes really exist, discovered rather than invented.
For Plato, the world we see is a copy; the original can only be grasped by thinking.

cards.title: Aristóteles
cards.text: Aristóteles (384–322 a.C.), aluno de Platão, estudou quase tudo: lógica, biologia, física, política, poesia. Foi tutor de Alexandre, o Grande, e fundou o Liceu.

deep.x: Aristotle was born in Stagira in northern Greece in 384 BCE. At about 17 he joined Plato's Academy in Athens and stayed for roughly 20 years. Later, King Philip of Macedon hired him to tutor his teenage son, the future Alexander the Great.
A different temperament

Where Plato looked up to the Forms, Aristotle looked down at the world. He dissected animals, classified hundreds of species and collected the constitutions of over 150 Greek cities. For him, the form of a thing lives inside it: the form of an oak is in the acorn, guiding its growth.
His legacy

x: Invented formal logic: the syllogism ruled for over 2,000 years
Founded biology as a careful, observational study
Wrote on ethics, politics, rhetoric, poetry and physics
Medieval Islamic and Christian scholars called him simply "the Philosopher"

deep.x: His followers were called **Peripatetics**, perhaps because he taught while walking in the Lyceum's covered walkways. What survives, about 30 works, are mostly lecture notes; his polished writings are lost.

deep.w: Aristotle's science was simply wrong
deep.r: Much of his physics failed, but his biology was so careful that Darwin admired it

deep.x: Aristotle brought philosophy down from heaven to look closely at the living world.

cards.title: O justo meio
cards.text: Para Aristóteles, a virtude fica entre dois extremos. A coragem está entre a covardia e a imprudência; a generosidade, entre a mesquinhez e o desperdício.

deep.x: In the *Nicomachean Ethics*, Aristotle describes a virtue as a settled habit of feeling and acting well. Each virtue sits between two vices: one of too much and one of too little.
Not the exact middle

The mean is "relative to us", not a mathematical average. Aristotle's example: if 10 kilos of food is too much and 2 too little, a trainer won't prescribe 6 to everyone; a champion wrestler needs more than a beginner. Likewise, the courageous response to a fire differs for a firefighter and a child.

Sometimes the right action is close to one extreme. Fury may be right in the face of cruelty. The mean is whatever the situation calls for, at the right time, towards the right people, for the right reason.
How you get there
You become brave by doing brave things, as you become a guitarist by playing. Aristotle's practical wisdom, **phronesis**, is the skill of seeing what each situation requires.

deep.w: The golden mean means always being moderate
deep.r: Some acts, like murder, have no right amount; and sometimes strong emotion is the mean

deep.x: Virtue is not the midpoint, but the right amount for this moment.

cards.title: Eudaimonia
cards.text: Para Aristóteles, o objetivo da vida era a eudaimonia, muitas vezes traduzida como florescimento: viver bem usando a razão e praticando a virtude, e não apenas se sentir bem.

deep.x: The Greek word joins **eu** (good) and **daimon** (spirit). Translating it as "happiness" misleads, because Aristotle didn't mean a pleasant mood. He meant a whole life going well: flourishing, as a plant thrives when it grows into what it can be.
The function argument

A knife's function is to cut, so a good knife cuts well. Aristotle asked what is distinctive about humans. Plants grow; animals feel; only humans reason. So a good human life is one of reasoning and acting well, which means practising virtue, over a whole lifetime.
What it needs

x: Virtue of character and practical wisdom
Friends, which Aristotle discusses at great length
Some luck and resources: health, enough money, a decent city
Time: one good day no more makes a flourishing life than one swallow makes a spring

deep.x: Objections

Critics ask whether humans really have one function, and whether a cruel tyrant who feels great is really failing. Aristotle's list of needs also excluded slaves and women from full flourishing, a view now universally rejected.
Modern psychologists distinguish "hedonic" well-being (pleasure) from "eudaimonic" well-being (purpose and growth), borrowing Aristotle's word.
A flourishing life is something you do, not something you feel.

cards.title: O método socrático hoje

items: O que você quer dizer com isso?
O que faria você mudar de ideia?

cards.text: Professores, advogados e coaches ainda usam o questionamento socrático: em vez de dar respostas, eles fazem perguntas que ajudam você a examinar seu próprio raciocínio.

deep.x: Socrates' style of questioning is called **elenchus**, Greek for "cross-examination". In Plato's *Euthyphro*, Socrates meets a man prosecuting his own father and asks him what piety is. Every definition collapses under follow-up questions. The dialogue ends without an answer, but with clearer thinking.
Where you meet it

x: **Law schools**: in the US, professors grill students on cases rather than lecture
**Therapy**: cognitive behavioural therapy uses Socratic questions to test anxious thoughts
**Teaching**: guiding a pupil to discover a rule rather than telling it
**Coaching and management**: "What would success look like?"
Thought: "I'll fail this exam"
Q: What's the evidence? "I struggled with one topic."
Q: How did you do last time? "I passed."
Revised: "I need to revise one topic."

deep.x: Good Socratic questioning is curious, not a trap. Done badly, it can feel like humiliation, as many of Socrates' victims found.
The best teachers don't hand you answers; they hand you better questions.

quiz.explain: Conhecer seus limites é o começo da sabedoria.

lessons.title: Ética
lessons.summary: Como devemos decidir o que é certo?

cards.title: Três grandes teorias
cards.text: A maioria das teorias éticas se concentra em uma de três coisas: as consequências de uma ação, os deveres ou regras envolvidos, ou o caráter de quem age.

deep.x: Ethics asks what makes actions right or wrong and what kind of person to be. Most modern theories fall into three families, each spotlighting a different part of any action.
One case, three lenses
Suppose you could lie to a friend to spare their feelings about a bad haircut.

x: A **consequentialist** asks: which choice leads to the most well-being overall?
A **deontologist** asks: is there a duty not to lie, whatever the result?
A **virtue ethicist** asks: what would an honest, kind person do here?

deep.x: The three often agree: torturing for fun is wrong on every view. They split on hard cases, which is where they get tested.
Each has a classic weakness

x: Consequentialism can seem to justify terrible acts if the sums work out
Duty theories can seem rigid when rules clash or disaster looms
Virtue ethics can seem vague: "do what a good person would" isn't always a clear instruction

deep.x: Many philosophers mix elements. Doctors, for example, weigh outcomes, respect patients' rights and value professional character all at once.
The word "consequentialism" was coined only in 1958, by the British philosopher Elizabeth Anscombe, who was criticising it.
Every ethical theory is a spotlight: it shows one part of the moral picture brightly and leaves another in shadow.

cards.title: Utilitarismo
cards.text: Jeremy Bentham e John Stuart Mill defenderam que a ação certa é aquela que produz a maior felicidade para o maior número de pessoas.

deep.x: Jeremy Bentham (1748–1832) was a London reformer who wanted laws judged by one test: do they increase happiness and reduce suffering? He counted everyone equally, including animals: the question, he said, is not whether they can reason but whether they can suffer.
Mill's refinement

John Stuart Mill (1806–1873), in *Utilitarianism* (1861), added that pleasures differ in quality. Poetry and friendship count for more than idle amusement: better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.

x: Option A: 4 people gain 5 units
Option B: 10 people gain 3 units
Utilitarian pick: B

deep.x: Strengths

x: Impartial: your happiness counts no more than a stranger's
Practical: it underlies cost–benefit analysis and public-health planning
Drove reforms: Bentham and Mill backed votes for women and an end to slavery

deep.x: The objections

Can you really measure and add happiness? Could the sums justify punishing an innocent person to calm a mob? And if every euro you spend on luxuries could save lives abroad, as Peter Singer argues, utilitarianism may demand almost everything you have. Defenders reply with refinements such as "rule utilitarianism": follow rules that, generally obeyed, do the most good.
Bentham's preserved skeleton, dressed in his clothes and topped with a wax head, sits in a glass case at University College London, as he requested.
Utilitarianism asks one simple question with a hard answer: what does the most good?

cards.title: O dever em Kant

items.r: "E se todos mentissem quando convém? A confiança desaba"

cards.text: Immanuel Kant defendeu que certas coisas são erradas sejam quais forem as consequências. O teste dele: aja apenas segundo uma regra que você pudesse querer que todos seguissem.

deep.x: Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) spent his whole life in Königsberg, a Prussian city now Kaliningrad in Russia. In the *Groundwork* (1785) he argued that morality can't rest on consequences, which are uncertain, but on reason itself.
Two kinds of "ought"

A **hypothetical imperative** says: if you want X, do Y. "If you want to pass, study." A **categorical imperative** says: do this, full stop. Kant thought moral rules are categorical: they bind you whatever you happen to want.
The universal law test
Before acting, state your rule ("maxim") and imagine everyone following it.

x: Maxim: borrow money with a false promise to repay
Universalise: everyone makes false promises
Result: nobody believes promises, so the trick can't work
Verdict: wrong

deep.x: The famous objection

A murderer knocks and asks where your friend is hiding. Kant, in a 1797 essay, said you still must not lie. Most readers find that wrong. Kantians reply that he misapplied his own theory, or that the rule can be framed more precisely: "never lie except to someone planning murder" might pass the test.

deep.w: Kant only cared about rules
deep.r: He cared about motive: an act has moral worth when done from duty, not merely in line with it

deep.x: Before you act, ask whether you could live in a world where everyone did the same.

cards.title: As pessoas como fins
cards.text: Kant também disse: nunca trate as pessoas apenas como meios para os seus objetivos, mas sempre também como fins em si mesmas, com a sua própria dignidade.

deep.x: Kant gave a second version of his supreme principle, now called the **formula of humanity**: treat humanity, in yourself and others, never merely as a means, always also as an end.
"Merely" is the key word

We use people as means all the time. You use the baker to get bread, and the baker uses you to earn a living. That's fine, because both of you agree and your goals are respected. What's wrong is treating someone like a tool: deceiving, manipulating or coercing them so their own choices don't count.
Dignity, not price

Kant said things in the world have either a price, which can be swapped for an equivalent, or **dignity**, which cannot. People have dignity because they can set their own goals. You can't trade one person's rights for another's convenience.
The objections

What about beings who can't make rational choices, like infants, people with severe dementia, or animals? Kant's theory struggles to explain their moral status, and many Kantians have tried to extend it. Others ask where exactly "persuasion" ends and "manipulation" begins, a question now central to debates about advertising and app design.
The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU, binding since 2009, opens with "Human dignity is inviolable", a strongly Kantian idea.
People are not tools; they have their own goals, and those goals count.

cards.title: Ética das virtudes
cards.text: Em vez de perguntar "que regra se aplica?", a ética das virtudes pergunta "o que uma boa pessoa faria?" e se concentra em cultivar traços como a honestidade, a coragem e a bondade.

deep.x: Virtue ethics goes back to Aristotle, Confucius and the Stoics. It faded in modern Europe but returned after Elizabeth Anscombe's 1958 essay argued that moral philosophy had lost its way by obsessing over rules. Philippa Foot, Alasdair MacIntyre and Rosalind Hursthouse developed it further.
Shifting the question
Rule-based theories ask "what should I do?" Virtue ethics asks "who should I be?" Right action follows from good character, the way good playing follows from skill.
Main virtues and their role
Strengths

x: Fits how moral life feels: we admire people, not just acts
Explains moral growth and moral education
Handles nuance: honesty with tact differs from bluntness

deep.x: Objections

Critics say it gives poor guidance in a dilemma: if you don't know what a virtuous person would do, being told to do it doesn't help. Lists of virtues also vary across cultures. Defenders answer that rules also need judgement to apply, and that virtues like honesty and courage appear in nearly every tradition.

Psychology research on "situationism" found that small things, like being in a hurry, can affect whether people help a stranger. Some philosophers think this challenges the idea of stable character; others disagree.
Good rules help, but in the end it's good people who apply them well.

cards.title: O dilema do bonde
cards.text: Um bonde desgovernado vai matar cinco pessoas. Você pode puxar uma alavanca para desviá-lo, matando uma pessoa no lugar delas. A maioria puxaria. Mas você empurraria alguém de uma ponte para pará-lo? A maioria diz que não.

deep.x: Philosopher Philippa Foot introduced the basic case in 1967 to discuss abortion law and the doctrine of double effect. Judith Jarvis Thomson named it the "trolley problem" and added the bridge version in the 1970s and 1980s.
Why the difference?
In both cases one dies and five live, so pure outcome-counting treats them alike. Yet intuitions split sharply. Proposed explanations:

x: **Double effect**: harm foreseen as a side-effect can be allowed; harm intended as a means cannot
**Using a person**: pushing treats him as a tool, echoing Kant
**Personal force**: pushing with your own hands triggers stronger emotional alarms

deep.x: Psychologist Joshua Greene scanned brains during these dilemmas and found that personal cases engage emotional areas more. He argued intuitions against pushing are fast gut reactions; critics reply that gut reactions can track real moral differences.
Beyond the classroom

Self-driving cars made it practical. MIT's online "Moral Machine" collected about 40 million choices from people in over 200 countries and territories, published in 2018, and found broad agreement on sparing more lives but cultural differences in detail.

deep.w: The trolley problem is just a silly puzzle
deep.r: It isolates one variable at a time, like a lab experiment for moral principles

deep.x: The same outcome can feel right or wrong depending on how you bring it about.

cards.title: Sorte moral
cards.text: Dois motoristas mandam mensagens ao volante; um atropela uma criança, o outro chega em casa em segurança. As escolhas foram igualmente ruins, mas os julgamos de forma muito diferente.

deep.x: Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel named this puzzle in 1976. We believe people should be judged only for what is under their control. Yet our judgements constantly depend on luck.

x: Driver A texts, glances up, reaches home
Driver B texts, glances up, a child runs out
Same choice, same risk
A gets a fine at most; B may face prison and lifelong blame

deep.x: Kinds of moral luck

items.b: how things happen to turn out
the tests life puts you to

deep.x: Circumstantial luck is chilling. Many ordinary people in 1930s Germany did terrible things they would never have faced in another country. Would you have been different? You can't know.
The law agrees with luck

Most legal systems, Portugal's included, punish an attempted crime less than a completed one, even when the intent was identical. Drunk driving is punished, but drunk driving that kills is punished far more.
Responses

Some say we should judge only intentions and risks, and treat the different outcomes as legally useful but morally irrelevant. Others accept moral luck as a real feature of life: we are agents in a world we don't control.

Williams's famous example was a painter like Gauguin who abandons his family for his art. Whether he was justified, Williams suggested, may depend on whether he becomes a great painter, which is partly luck.
We think blame should follow choices, but in practice it follows results.

cards.title: O véu da ignorância
cards.text: John Rawls perguntou: que sociedade você projetaria se não soubesse quem seria nela, rico ou pobre, saudável ou doente? Ele achava que você protegeria os mais desfavorecidos.

deep.x: John Rawls (1921–2002), a Harvard philosopher, set out this thought experiment in *A Theory of Justice* (1971), one of the most discussed books in modern political philosophy.
The original position

Imagine choosing the basic rules of your society from behind a veil that hides your sex, class, talents, health, religion and ethnicity. Because you can't rig the rules for yourself, Rawls argued, whatever you'd choose there counts as fair.
Rawls's two principles

x: Equal basic liberties for all: speech, conscience, vote, fair trial
Fair equality of opportunity for jobs and positions
The **difference principle**: inequalities are allowed only if they benefit the worst off

deep.x: In this illustration, Rawls would pick B even if A or C had a higher average income, because B's worst-off group does best.
Strong objections

x: John Harsanyi argued that rational choosers would maximise average welfare, not insure against the worst case
Robert Nozick (*Anarchy, State, and Utopia*, 1974) argued that justice depends on how wealth was acquired, not on its pattern
Communitarians such as Michael Sandel said nobody really chooses as a "person" stripped of all ties

deep.x: The idea of fair division by ignorance is old: "I cut, you choose" for sharing a cake works on the same logic.
If you didn't know where you'd land, which society would you want to live in?

cards.title: Ser e dever ser

steps: Fato: fumar faz mal à saúde

cards.text: David Hume percebeu que não se tira um "deve" apenas de um "é". "Fumar faz mal à saúde" não significa, por si só, "você não deve fumar"; é preciso também um valor.

deep.x: Scottish philosopher David Hume (1711–1776), in his *Treatise of Human Nature* (1739–40), noticed that authors often move from statements about what **is** the case to what **ought** to be, without explaining how. He doubted the jump can be made by logic alone.

items: Value: you ought to protect health

deep.x: The missing premise
Facts alone can't produce an "ought". To reach one, you need at least one premise that already contains a value. Often it's hidden because everyone shares it.

x: Fact: this bridge is unsafe
Hidden value: we should not put people at serious risk
Conclusion: we ought to close the bridge

deep.x: Where it bites

x: "It's natural, so it's good" (or "unnatural, so bad") skips the value premise
Evolution explains why we have certain urges; it doesn't show we should act on them
Data can tell us a policy's effects; deciding whether it's worth it needs values

items.w: Humans evolved to eat sugar, so we should
items.r: Evolution explains urges, not what's right

deep.x: Challenges

Some philosophers think Hume's gap can be bridged. John Searle argued in 1964 that "she promised" seems to imply "she ought to do it". Others say concepts like "cruel" or "rude" mix fact and value from the start.
This idea is often nicknamed "Hume's guillotine", because it seems to cut facts off from values.
Facts tell you how the world is; to say what you should do, you also need a value.

cards.title: Uma escolha difícil
cards.text: Uma médica tem cinco pacientes que precisam de órgãos e um visitante saudável. Uma soma utilitarista parece dizer para sacrificar um; quase todo mundo diz que não. Testar teorias com casos é como a ética avança.

deep.x: This "transplant" case, sharpened by Judith Jarvis Thomson in the 1970s, mirrors the trolley switch: kill one, save five. Yet almost nobody accepts the surgeon's choice, even people who would pull the trolley lever.
How each theory responds

x: **Kantian**: the visitor is used merely as a means; forbidden
**Rule utilitarian**: if hospitals did this, nobody would visit one; worse overall
**Virtue ethicist**: no good doctor could do this; it betrays the role
**Rights theorist**: the visitor's right to life is a barrier, not a number

deep.x: Reflective equilibrium
Rawls described a method for ethics that resembles science. Principles are like theories; strong case judgements are like data. When they clash, you adjust one or the other until they fit.

This is why philosophers invent strange cases. They isolate one factor at a time. If a theory says "sacrifice the visitor", that's evidence against the theory, just as a failed prediction counts against a scientific hypothesis.

deep.w: Thought experiments are unrealistic, so useless
deep.r: Real cases mix many factors; simple cases show which one is doing the work

deep.x: Ethics advances when theories meet hard cases and have to change.

quiz.q: Qual teoria julga as ações pelas suas consequências?
quiz.explain: A maior felicidade para o maior número.

quiz.q: O que é o "véu da ignorância" de Rawls?
options: Projetar a sociedade sem saber o seu lugar nela

cards.title: A dúvida de Descartes
cards.text: René Descartes tentou duvidar de tudo: os sentidos podem enganar, os sonhos parecem reais. A única coisa de que ele não conseguia duvidar era de que estava duvidando: "Penso, logo existo."

deep.x: René Descartes (1596–1650) was a French mathematician who invented the coordinate graph (x and y axes). He wanted knowledge as solid as geometry, so in his *Meditations* (1641) he decided to tear everything down and rebuild only on what could not possibly be doubted.

items: An evil demon could fool me

deep.x: Three waves of doubt

x: Senses deceive: a straight stick looks bent in water
Dreams: while dreaming you are convinced it's real, so how can you be sure now?
The evil demon: imagine a powerful deceiver feeding you false experiences, even in maths

deep.x: The one certainty

Even if a demon deceives me, I must exist to be deceived. Doubting is a kind of thinking, and thinking needs a thinker. Hence *cogito, ergo sum*: I think, therefore I am. The French version, "je pense, donc je suis", appeared first, in his *Discourse on Method* (1637).
Objections

x: Critics such as Georg Lichtenberg said Descartes was only entitled to "there is thinking", not to an "I"
To rebuild the world, Descartes relied on a proof that a good God wouldn't deceive us, and his proof of God relied on clear ideas, which looked circular to many readers

deep.x: Descartes died in Stockholm in 1650, a few months after moving there to tutor Queen Christina, who wanted lessons at 5 a.m. in a freezing winter.
When you doubt everything, the doubter is still left standing.

cards.title: Racionalistas vs. empiristas
cards.text: Racionalistas como Descartes diziam que o conhecimento vem principalmente da razão. Empiristas como Locke e Hume diziam que ele vem da experiência; a mente começa como uma folha em branco.

deep.x: In the 1600s and 1700s, European philosophy split over a simple question: where does knowledge come from?
The rationalist case
Some truths seem knowable without looking: 7 + 5 = 12, or every event has a cause. Descartes thought ideas like God and infinity couldn't come from experience and must be innate.
The empiricist case

John Locke's *Essay Concerning Human Understanding* (1689) compared the newborn mind to white paper, often called a **tabula rasa** or blank slate. Everything is written there by sensation and reflection. Hume pushed this hard: if an idea can't be traced back to an impression, it's suspect.
Kant's compromise

Immanuel Kant argued in the *Critique of Pure Reason* (1781) that both were partly right. Knowledge begins with experience, but the mind supplies the structure, such as space, time and cause, that makes experience possible at all.

Locke discussed "Molyneux's problem": could a blind person who regained sight recognise a cube by sight alone? A 2011 study of children treated for congenital blindness in India found they at first couldn't, but learned within days.

deep.w: Empiricists thought the mind does nothing
deep.r: Locke and Hume gave the mind powers to compare, combine and reflect; they denied only built-in ideas

deep.x: Kant's lesson: experience gives the content, the mind gives the shape.

cards.title: O problema da indução
cards.text: O Sol nasceu todos os dias, então esperamos que ele nasça amanhã. Hume apontou que não podemos provar que o futuro será como o passado; simplesmente supomos isso.

deep.x: David Hume set out the problem in the *Treatise* (1739) and his *Enquiry* (1748). Every prediction from experience rests on one assumption: that nature will continue as before. But how do we know that?
The circle

You can't prove it by logic, because a world where the Sun stops is perfectly imaginable. You can't prove it by experience either: "induction has worked in the past, so it will work in the future" uses induction to defend induction.
Russell's chicken
Bertrand Russell (1912) described a chicken fed by the farmer every morning. Each day its confidence grows. Then one morning the farmer wrings its neck. More data made the chicken surer, not safer.
Responses

x: Hume himself: we can't justify it, but we can't help doing it; it's custom, and life needs it
Popper: science doesn't need induction, only bold guesses and tests
Probability theorists: we can't be certain, but evidence can rationally raise our confidence

deep.x: Financial crises are a modern chicken story: models trained on years of calm data often fail exactly when conditions change.
No amount of past evidence logically guarantees the future, yet we have no better guide.

cards.title: Falseabilidade

items.r: "Que resultado a refutaria?"

cards.text: Karl Popper defendeu que uma teoria científica precisa ser testável de um jeito que possa provar que ela está errada. "Todos os cisnes são brancos" é científica: um cisne negro a refuta.

deep.x: Karl Popper (1902–1994) grew up in Vienna, where in 1919 he noticed a contrast. Freud's and Adler's theories seemed to explain every possible behaviour, while Einstein's relativity made a risky prediction about starlight bending near the Sun, which could have failed.
The asymmetry

No number of white swans proves that all swans are white. But one black swan proves that not all are. Europeans thought this was settled until Dutch explorers saw black swans in Western Australia in 1697.
The criterion

Popper's *Logic of Scientific Discovery* (German 1934, English 1959) proposed that a theory is scientific only if some possible observation could contradict it. This isn't about whether it's true; it's about whether it takes a risk.

items.b: Water boils at 100 °C at sea level

deep.x: Criticisms

Real tests are messy. When a prediction fails, scientists can blame an auxiliary assumption instead of the main theory, and sometimes they're right to. Philosophers Pierre Duhem and W. V. O. Quine stressed that theories always face tests as a bundle.

deep.w: A theory that explains everything is very strong
deep.r: If no observation could ever count against it, it tells you nothing about the world

deep.x: A good theory sticks its neck out: it says what you should never see.

cards.title: O problema mente–corpo
cards.text: Como o cérebro físico produz pensamentos e sentimentos? Os dualistas dizem que mente e corpo são coisas diferentes; os fisicalistas dizem que a mente é o que o cérebro faz.

deep.x: You decide to raise your arm, and it rises. A thought seems to move matter. But thoughts don't have mass or position the way neurons do. How do the two connect?
Descartes' dualism
Descartes argued the mind is a non-physical thinking thing, separate from the extended body. He suggested they interact via the pineal gland in the brain.
In 1643, Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia wrote him a sharp question: how can something without size or contact push something physical? His answers never fully satisfied her, or later philosophers.
The main positions

x: **Substance dualism**: mind and body are two kinds of thing
**Property dualism**: one kind of thing, the brain, but with irreducible mental properties
**Physicalism**: the mind is entirely physical; mental states are brain states or functions
**Idealism**: reality is fundamentally mental; matter depends on mind

deep.x: Evidence from the brain

Brain damage changes personality, memory and judgement. In 1848, railway worker Phineas Gage survived an iron rod through his frontal lobe, and friends said he was "no longer Gage". Physicalists see such cases as strong support. Dualists reply that a damaged instrument can't play well, even if the player is separate.
Every view must explain how the felt life of the mind fits with the physical brain, and none does so effortlessly.

cards.title: O problema difícil

items.b: por que se sente como algo

cards.text: O filósofo David Chalmers perguntou por que a atividade cerebral é sentida de algum modo. Explicar o que o cérebro faz é "fácil"; explicar por que existe uma experiência interior é "difícil".

deep.x: David Chalmers named it in a 1995 paper after a talk at a 1994 consciousness conference in Tucson, Arizona. The talk became one of the most cited ideas in modern philosophy of mind.
Why "easy" isn't easy

The easy problems may take centuries, but we know what an answer looks like: find the mechanism that performs the function. For the hard problem, even a complete map of the mechanisms seems to leave a question: why isn't all that processing happening "in the dark"?
Zombies

Chalmers asks you to imagine a philosophical zombie: an exact physical copy of you that behaves identically but has no inner experience. If that is even coherent, he argues, experience is something extra to physical facts.

items: Illusionism: the problem is a trick

deep.x: Pushback

Daniel Dennett argued the hard problem is an illusion produced by how the brain models itself, and that zombies are not truly conceivable. Others think it will dissolve as neuroscience matures, as "what is life?" did in biology.
In 1998 neuroscientist Christof Koch bet Chalmers a case of wine that the brain basis of consciousness would be found within 25 years. In 2023 Koch conceded and paid up.
You can describe what a brain does without ever explaining why it feels like something.

cards.title: Como é ser um morcego?

steps: Saber tudo sobre cérebros de morcego

cards.text: Thomas Nagel defendeu que, mesmo sabendo tudo sobre a ecolocalização de um morcego, não saberíamos como é vivenciá-la por dentro.

deep.x: Thomas Nagel published this paper in 1974. He chose bats because they're mammals, so surely conscious, yet they perceive the world mainly through echolocation, a sense we lack.
The argument

A creature is conscious if there is "something it is like" to be it. Science describes from the outside, in an objective, third-person way. But the bat's experience is essentially first-person. Adding more outside facts never seems to give you the inside view.
Mary's room

Frank Jackson's 1982 version: Mary is a brilliant scientist who knows every physical fact about colour vision but has lived her whole life in a black-and-white room. When she first sees a red tomato, does she learn something new? If yes, physical facts weren't everything.
Replies

x: Some say Mary gains a new ability (to recognise and imagine red), not a new fact
Others say she meets an old fact in a new way, as you can know "water" and "H₂O" separately
Jackson himself later changed his mind and became a physicalist

deep.w: Nagel argued minds are non-physical
deep.r: He argued our current concepts can't yet explain experience, and left physicalism possibly true but not understood

deep.x: Knowing everything about a mind from outside may still leave out what it's like inside.

cards.title: O quarto chinês
cards.text: John Searle imaginou uma pessoa que segue um livro de regras para responder perfeitamente a perguntas em chinês sem entender chinês. Um computador entende, ou só manipula símbolos?

deep.x: John Searle published the thought experiment in 1980 to challenge "strong AI", the claim that a correctly programmed computer literally understands.
The argument

The man in the room doesn't know Chinese. He matches symbols by their shape. Outsiders think a fluent speaker is inside. A computer, Searle said, does the same: it manipulates symbols by rules (**syntax**) with no grasp of what they mean (**semantics**). Syntax alone isn't enough for meaning.
The famous replies

Searle replied to the systems reply: let the man memorise the whole rulebook. He is now the whole system, and he still doesn't understand. Critics answer that our intuitions about something so huge and slow are unreliable.
Its link to Turing

Alan Turing's 1950 "imitation game" proposed judging machine intelligence by behaviour in conversation. Searle's room is designed to pass that test while lacking understanding, to show behaviour isn't enough.
A real rulebook for conversation would be astronomically large, and the man would take years per answer. Defenders of AI say this hides how different the real system is.
Searle's question: can following rules ever add up to understanding?

cards.title: Identidade pessoal

events.l: todas as tábuas novas, mesmo navio?

cards.text: Se cada tábua de um navio for substituída com o tempo, ele continua sendo o mesmo navio? Suas células também se renovam. O que faz de você a mesma pessoa ao longo da vida: a memória, o corpo ou outra coisa?

deep.x: The ancient Greek writer Plutarch told of the ship of Theseus, kept in Athens with rotting planks replaced one by one. Thomas Hobbes added a twist: suppose someone collects the old planks and rebuilds them. Which is the real ship?
Theories of personal identity

x: **Body**: you are your living organism
**Memory**: John Locke (1694) said you are the same person as far back as your consciousness reaches
**Psychological continuity**: overlapping chains of memories, beliefs and intentions
**No-self**: Buddhists and Hume doubted there's a fixed self at all

deep.x: Reid's officer

Thomas Reid attacked Locke's memory theory. A boy is flogged; as a young officer he remembers the flogging; as an old general he remembers being an officer but not the flogging. By Locke's rule, the general is the officer and the officer is the boy, yet the general is not the boy. Most theorists now use overlapping chains instead.
Parfit's teleporter

Derek Parfit (*Reasons and Persons*, 1984) imagined a teleporter that scans you, destroys you and builds an exact copy on Mars. Is it travel or death? He concluded identity may matter less than we think; what matters is continuity of psychology.

deep.w: All your cells are replaced every seven years
deep.r: Many are, but most neurons in your cerebral cortex and the cells in your eye's lens stay with you for life

deep.x: You change constantly, yet something keeps you "you", and philosophers still disagree about what.

cards.title: Pensando sobre a IA
cards.text: Esses velhos enigmas agora são práticos: um modelo de linguagem pode entender, ou ter experiências? Os filósofos discordam, e o quarto chinês é citado em debates sobre IA toda semana.

deep.x: Large language models, released widely from 2022, write essays and hold conversations that easily pass casual versions of Turing's test. That turned old thought experiments into live questions for engineers, regulators and the public.
The understanding debate

x: Searle-style sceptics: models predict the next word from statistics; impressive syntax, no meaning
Functionalists: if a system uses information in the right ways, that just is understanding
Middle views: understanding comes in degrees, and models may have some kinds but not others

deep.x: The consciousness debate

In 2022 a Google engineer said a chatbot was sentient; most experts disagreed. In 2023, a group of scientists and philosophers published a report listing "indicator properties" drawn from theories of consciousness, and judged that no current system was a strong candidate, while seeing no obvious barrier to building one.

items: treat a tool as a person

deep.x: Why it matters in practice

The EU's AI Act (2024) regulates AI by risk and requires that people be told when they're talking to a chatbot. Questions of responsibility, deception and trust don't wait for the deep metaphysics to be settled.
Some philosophers argue we may never be sure whether a system is conscious, because the hard problem leaves no test that everyone accepts.
Old puzzles about minds now have to be answered about machines we use every day.

quiz.q: Do que Descartes não conseguia duvidar?
Segundo Popper, uma teoria científica precisa ser…

cards.title: Estoicismo
cards.text: Estoicos como Epicteto, Sêneca e Marco Aurélio ensinavam que não controlamos os acontecimentos, só nossos julgamentos e ações. A paz vem de nos concentrarmos no que depende de nós.

deep.x: The school began around 300 BCE when Zeno of Citium taught at the Stoa Poikile, the "painted porch" in Athens, which gave it its name. It flourished for 500 years and reached its most read writers under the Roman Empire.
Core ideas

x: Virtue (wisdom, justice, courage, self-control) is the only true good
Wealth, health and fame are "preferred indifferents": nice, but not needed for a good life
Emotions like rage and panic come from mistaken judgements, which we can examine
Humans are part of one rational cosmos and owe something to all people, not just their city

deep.x: A living influence

In the 1950s and 60s, psychologists Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck, founders of what became cognitive behavioural therapy, credited Epictetus's insight that we're upset not by things but by our opinions about them.
Objections

Critics ancient and modern ask whether Stoicism asks too much. Should a grieving parent really treat their child's death as "indifferent"? And focusing on your inner attitude might make people too accepting of injustice that could be changed.

deep.w: Stoic means emotionless
deep.r: Stoics aimed to replace destructive passions with good emotions like joy, care and calm resolve

deep.x: Stoicism trains the one thing always in your power: how you respond.

cards.title: A dicotomia do controle
cards.text: Antes de se preocupar, classifique o problema: posso controlá-lo, influenciá-lo ou nenhuma das duas coisas? Gaste energia só com as duas primeiras.

deep.x: The *Enchiridion* ("handbook"), a summary of Epictetus's teaching made by his student Arrian, opens with this idea. Some things are up to us: our opinions, choices, desires and aversions. Others are not: our body, property, reputation and status.
The middle category
Modern writers like William Irvine (2009) add a third box: things we can **influence** but not control. You can't control whether you win a match, but you can control how well you train and play.
The Stoic archer

Cicero described the Stoic view with an archer. Her goal is to shoot well: choose the bow, aim carefully, release cleanly. Once the arrow leaves, wind may carry it off. Hitting the target is preferred, but shooting well is the real aim.

x: Job interview tomorrow
Control: prepare, sleep, arrive early
Influence: first impression
Neither: other candidates, the final decision
Spend tonight on the first box

deep.x: Objections

Drawing the line is not always easy, and people sometimes underrate their influence on politics, health or work. Critics worry the method could become an excuse for passivity. Stoics answered that duty to others is firmly "up to us".
The 20th-century "Serenity Prayer" (grant me the serenity to accept what I cannot change…) expresses a very similar idea in religious form.
Put your energy where it can change something, and let the rest go.

cards.title: Visualização negativa
cards.text: Os estoicos imaginavam perder o que tinham, não para ficarem tristes, mas para valorizarem mais o que tinham e estarem preparados para os contratempos.

deep.x: The Latin name is **premeditatio malorum**, "the premeditation of evils". Seneca recommended imagining exile, illness or loss in advance, so that if they arrived they would hurt less and would not come as a shock.
Two goals

x: **Gratitude**: we stop noticing what we have; imagining its loss makes it vivid again
**Resilience**: the mind rehearses the blow, so it lands softer

deep.x: Psychologists call the first problem **hedonic adaptation**: a new phone or job thrills us, then quickly becomes normal. Negative visualisation is a deliberate counter-move.
Voluntary discomfort
Seneca also suggested spending a few days a month on plain food and rough clothes, asking yourself "is this what I feared?" Modern versions include cold showers or a day without the phone.
Use with care

For people prone to anxiety, dwelling on disaster can backfire. The Stoic version is short, purposeful and ends in action and gratitude. Business uses a cousin of it: the "pre-mortem", where a team imagines a project has failed and asks why.
Epictetus suggested that when kissing your child goodnight you quietly remember they are mortal. It sounds bleak, but his point was to love them more fully today.
Imagining loss briefly is a way to treasure what you have now.

cards.title: Epicurismo
cards.text: Epicuro ensinava que uma vida boa é uma vida agradável, mas se referia a prazeres simples: amigos, conversa, pão e água, e ausência de medo e dor, não ao luxo.

deep.x: Epicurus (341–270 BCE) bought a house with a garden outside Athens and founded a community there, unusually admitting women and slaves. His school was called simply "the Garden".
Pleasure, properly understood

For Epicurus, the goal of life is pleasure, but he defined the best pleasure as the absence of pain in the body (**aponia**) and of trouble in the mind (**ataraxia**). Feasts and fame bring anxiety; a quiet life with friends brings lasting calm.
The four-part cure
His followers summarised the teaching as a "four-part remedy":

x: Don't fear the gods: they don't punish or reward
Don't fear death: when death is, we are not
What is good is easy to get
What is terrible is easy to endure

deep.x: Science against fear

Epicurus adopted Democritus's atoms. If everything, including the soul, is atoms that scatter at death, there is no afterlife to fear. The Roman poet Lucretius spread these ideas in *On the Nature of Things*, a poem rediscovered in 1417 that influenced Renaissance science.
Objections

Critics, from Stoics to Christian writers, said a life aimed at one's own calm is too self-centred and ignores duty. Others doubt that death is truly nothing to us: we can lose future goods even if we don't feel the loss.

deep.w: An epicure is a lover of luxury
deep.r: Epicurus lived on bread, water and olives, and once asked a friend for a little pot of cheese as a treat

deep.x: The pleasant life is simple: good friends, few needs, no unnecessary fears.

cards.title: Filosofia budista
cards.text: Buda ensinou que o sofrimento vem do desejo e do apego, e que um caminho de vida ética, atenção plena e sabedoria pode levar além dele.

deep.x: Siddhartha Gautama was born a prince, probably in the 5th century BCE, at Lumbini in what is now Nepal; scholars debate the exact dates. Shocked by old age, sickness and death, he left home to seek an answer. After years of extreme fasting, he decided harsh self-denial was no better than luxury.
Three marks of existence

x: **Impermanence** (anicca): everything that arises passes away
**Unsatisfactoriness** (dukkha): what is impermanent can't give lasting satisfaction
**Non-self** (anatta): no fixed, unchanging self lies beneath our experiences

deep.x: Philosophy or religion?

Buddhism includes rituals, monasteries and beliefs about rebirth, which make it a religion for about 500 million people. But much of its core is philosophical: careful analysis of mind, causes and the self, offered to be tested in experience rather than taken on authority.
Questions and objections

Critics ask whether "non-self" is coherent: who is it that suffers and seeks liberation? Buddhist philosophers developed subtle answers about selves as useful labels for changing processes. Some Western readers also worry the goal of ending desire sounds like ending engagement; Buddhists reply the aim is ending clinging, not caring.
The Buddha's first sermon, in a deer park at Sarnath near Varanasi, is said to have been given to five former companions who had abandoned him for giving up fasting.
The Buddha diagnosed suffering as a habit of grasping, and treated it with a way of living.

cards.title: Confúcio
cards.text: Confúcio (551–479 a.C.) valorizava as boas relações, o respeito, a educação e o aperfeiçoamento pessoal. Sua regra de ouro: "Não faça aos outros o que você não quer que façam com você."

deep.x: Kong Qiu, honoured as Kong Fuzi ("Master Kong") and Latinised as Confucius, lived in the small state of Lu in eastern China during an age of war between rival states. He worked as an official and teacher, and spent years travelling in search of a ruler who would govern by virtue. None fully took his advice.
The Analects
Confucius didn't write a book. His disciples later collected his sayings in the *Analects*, short exchanges full of practical wisdom about friendship, learning and government.
The negative golden rule

Asked for one word to guide a whole life, Confucius answered **shu**, reciprocity, and explained it as not doing to others what you don't want done to you. Similar rules appear in Greek, Jewish, Christian and Hindu sources.
Lasting influence

For about 1,300 years, China's civil service exams tested knowledge of the Confucian classics, so the ideas shaped everyone who governed. Critics, especially during China's May Fourth Movement of 1919, blamed Confucian hierarchy for holding back women and the young. Defenders stress its emphasis on education, merit and duty.
For Confucius, a good society begins with people who keep working on themselves.

cards.title: Existencialismo
cards.text: Jean-Paul Sartre disse que "a existência precede a essência": não nascemos com um propósito fixo; criamos a nós mesmos por meio das nossas escolhas e somos responsáveis por elas.

deep.x: Jean-Paul Sartre (1905–1980) gave a famous lecture in Paris in 1945, published as *Existentialism Is a Humanism*. His key example was a paper knife. A craftsman has the idea of a paper knife first, then makes it: its essence comes before its existence. Humans, Sartre said, are the reverse.
Condemned to be free
Without a fixed human nature or a designer's plan, we must choose, and even refusing to choose is a choice. That freedom brings **anguish** (we answer for what we make of ourselves) but also dignity.
Bad faith

Sartre's word for pretending you have no choice. His example was a café waiter acting a little too much like a waiter, playing a role as if it were his fixed nature. "That's just who I am" can be bad faith.
Objections

Simone de Beauvoir, Sartre's partner, argued in *The Second Sex* (1949) that freedom is shaped by circumstances such as gender and poverty: one is not born, but becomes, a woman. Others say Sartre ignored biology, culture and childhood. Religious thinkers reply that human nature and purpose may be real, and existentialism simply assumes otherwise.
Sartre was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1964 and turned it down, saying a writer should not let himself be turned into an institution.
You aren't handed a script; you write yourself through what you choose.

cards.title: O absurdo

steps: Empurrar de novo e achar alegria nisso

cards.text: Albert Camus descreveu o absurdo: nossa busca de sentido em um universo que não oferece nenhum. Sua resposta, em *O Mito de Sísifo*: continuar vivendo plenamente mesmo assim.

deep.x: Albert Camus (1913–1960) grew up poor in French Algeria. In *The Myth of Sisyphus* (1942) he described the absurd not as a property of the world, nor of humans, but of their meeting: we demand meaning and clarity, and the universe stays silent.
Three responses
Camus asked what follows from the absurd and considered three options.

He rejected the first because it ends the confrontation rather than facing it. He called the second "philosophical suicide": jumping to a comforting answer the evidence doesn't support. His choice was to keep the tension open and live with lucidity and passion.
Sisyphus

In Greek myth, Sisyphus is condemned to roll a boulder up a hill forever, only to watch it roll down. Camus pictures him walking back down, fully aware of his fate. In that awareness, he says, Sisyphus is greater than his rock.
Objections

Religious thinkers deny the universe is silent. Others ask why the absurd should lead to revolt rather than despair or indifference. Camus's answer is less a proof than an attitude: lucidity without false hope.

deep.w: Camus was an existentialist
deep.r: He rejected the label and distanced himself from Sartre; they publicly fell out in 1952

deep.x: Camus won the Nobel Prize in 1957, aged 44, and died in a car crash in France less than three years later.
The absurd isn't a reason to stop living; it's the background against which we choose to live.

cards.title: Os muitos eus de Pessoa
cards.text: O poeta português Fernando Pessoa escreveu como dezenas de "heterônimos", como Alberto Caeiro, Ricardo Reis e Álvaro de Campos, cada um com sua própria vida e filosofia.

deep.x: Fernando Pessoa (1888–1935) was born in Lisbon, grew up in Durban, South Africa, and wrote in Portuguese, English and French. He worked as a commercial translator and published only one Portuguese book in his lifetime, *Mensagem* (1934).

After his death, a trunk was found with more than 25,000 pages of manuscripts. Scholars are still editing it. Researchers have counted over 100 fictional authors in it, though only a few are fully developed.
Each with a philosophy

x: **Caeiro**, a shepherd-poet, rejects metaphysics: things are what they appear, no hidden meanings
**Reis**, a doctor exiled to Brazil, writes Horace-like odes with Stoic and Epicurean calm
**Campos**, trained in naval engineering in Glasgow, swings from wild enthusiasm for machines to deep weariness

deep.x: A philosophical experiment

Pessoa turned the question "who am I?" into literature. If one mind can host several coherent selves, maybe the unified self is more fragile than it feels. It echoes Hume's view of the self as a bundle of perceptions and the Buddhist idea of non-self.
Pessoa said the master Caeiro "appeared" on 8 March 1914, when he wrote over 30 poems in one standing session. Scholars think the story is at least partly invented.
Pessoa showed that a single person can contain many ways of seeing the world.

cards.title: Uma manhã estoica

items: Quem pode me pôr à prova?

cards.text: Toda manhã, Marco Aurélio lembrava a si mesmo que encontraria pessoas difíceis naquele dia, e que mesmo assim podia escolher agir bem. Um plano de um minuto para o dia que vem pela frente.

deep.x: Book 2 of Marcus Aurelius's *Meditations* opens with this reminder. He would meet people who were meddling, ungrateful, arrogant or deceitful. But they act from ignorance of good and bad, they share his human nature, and none of them can force him into acting badly.
Writing to himself

The *Meditations* were private notes, written in Greek, probably during military campaigns on the Danube in the 170s CE. Their Greek title translates as "to himself". He never meant them to be published.
Try it

x: Morning (1 min): who might be difficult today?
How do I want to act anyway?
Evening (2 min): what went well, what didn't, what next time?

deep.x: The evening review was recommended by Seneca, who described going over his day each night once the lamp was out, judging himself kindly but honestly.
Why it works

x: Expecting friction makes it less shocking, so anger has less fuel
Remembering shared humanity makes contempt harder
Fixing your intention in advance gives you a plan when emotions rise

deep.x: Marcus ruled during a devastating plague, probably smallpox, and near-constant war on the frontiers. His calm was hard-won, not easy.
Decide how you want to act before the day decides for you.

quiz.explain: Concentre-se no que depende de você.

cards.title: O que é um argumento
cards.text: Um argumento dá razões (premissas) para uma conclusão. Ele é bom se as premissas forem verdadeiras e de fato sustentarem a conclusão.

deep.x: In everyday speech an "argument" is a row. In logic it's something calmer: a set of statements where some (the **premises**) are offered as reasons to accept another (the **conclusion**).
Spotting the parts

Indicator words help. "Because", "since" and "given that" usually introduce premises. "So", "therefore" and "which means" usually introduce the conclusion. Many arguments hide a premise because it seems obvious.

x: "She's a vet, so she must love animals"
Hidden premise: all vets love animals
Is that premise true? Probably not always
The argument is weaker than it looks

deep.x: Two ways an argument can fail

x: A premise is false or doubtful
The premises, even if true, don't support the conclusion

deep.x: Why it's useful

Laying out premises turns a heated disagreement into a map. You can point to the exact step you dispute. Often people agree on more than they think and differ on one premise, about facts or about values.
Aristotle was the first to study the forms of arguments systematically, over 2,300 years ago; his system of syllogisms was taught in European universities until the 1800s.
To judge an argument, ask two questions: are the reasons true, and do they really support the claim?

cards.title: Válido vs. sólido
cards.text: Um argumento é válido se a conclusão decorre necessariamente das premissas; é sólido se for válido e as premissas forem verdadeiras. "Todos os gatos voam; Tom é um gato; logo, Tom voa" é válido, mas não é sólido.

deep.x: Logicians separate two questions. Is the reasoning structure right? That's **validity**. Are the premises also true? Then the argument is **sound**, and its conclusion must be true.

items.b: if premises true, conclusion must be

deep.x: Validity is about form
Validity doesn't care about content. These two arguments share a valid form:

x: All cats fly; Tom is a cat
So Tom flies (valid, unsound)
All humans are mortal; Ana is human
So Ana is mortal (valid, sound)

deep.x: The common form: all A are B; x is A; so x is B. Any argument with that shape is valid, whatever you plug in.
Surprising combinations
The right-hand argument has a true conclusion, but the premises don't guarantee it: by that logic, sparrows would swim too. A true conclusion doesn't make reasoning good.
A common trap
"If it rained, the street is wet. The street is wet. So it rained." This is invalid, called **affirming the consequent**: a street cleaner could have wet it.

items.w: If P then Q; Q; so P
items.r: If P then Q; P; so Q

deep.x: Validity is about the shape of reasoning; soundness adds the truth of what you start from.

cards.title: Dedução vs. indução
cards.text: A dedução vai de regras gerais a conclusões certas. A indução vai de observações a generalizações prováveis.

deep.x: These are two basic directions of reasoning, and most real thinking uses both.
Deduction

If all mammals have lungs and whales are mammals, then whales have lungs. If the premises are true, the conclusion can't be false. Mathematics is the great home of deduction. The price: the conclusion was already hidden in the premises.
Induction

Every swan you've seen is white, so all swans are white. Induction ventures beyond the evidence, which makes it useful and risky. Strength depends on sample size, variety and whether the sample is representative.

x: Survey 1,000 voters chosen at random
52% back a proposal
Typical margin of error about ±3 points
Conclusion: probably 49–55% of all voters

deep.x: A third type: abduction

Philosopher Charles Peirce named **abduction**, or inference to the best explanation. The lawn is wet and the sky is clear; the best explanation is that the sprinkler ran. Doctors diagnosing and detectives investigating rely on it.

deep.w: Sherlock Holmes is a master of deduction
deep.r: Most of Holmes's reasoning is abduction: guessing the best explanation from clues, which could be wrong

deep.x: Deduction keeps you safe but small; induction lets you learn but never guarantees.

cards.title: Ad hominem

items.r: Responda ao que ela de fato disse

cards.text: Atacar a pessoa em vez do argumento. "Você não pode confiar nos dados climáticos dele; ele dirige um carro grande" não diz nada sobre os dados.

deep.x: Latin for "to the person". The fallacy is rejecting a claim because of who makes it, rather than what is said. Data are true or false whatever the scientist drives.
Three common forms

x: **Abusive**: "Only an idiot would believe that"
**Circumstantial**: "Of course she supports the tax; she works in the public sector"
**Tu quoque** ("you too"): "You tell me not to smoke, but you smoke"

deep.x: The smoker case is a good test. Hypocrisy is a fair criticism of the person, but it doesn't make the advice wrong. Smoking harms the parent and the teenager alike.
When the person is relevant

Not every comment about a source is a fallacy. In court, a witness who lied before may be less credible. A study funded by a company selling the product deserves a closer look. The difference: these raise questions about **reliability**; they don't by themselves prove the claim false.

items.r: She may be biased, so check her evidence

deep.x: A related error, the **genetic fallacy**, judges an idea by its origin: "that idea came from a dictator, so it's bad".
Judge the argument, not the arguer; then, separately, ask how reliable the source is.

cards.title: Espantalho

items.r: Responder à posição real

cards.text: Distorcer a posição de alguém para que fique mais fácil de atacar. "Você quer limites de velocidade? Então quer que todo mundo ande a pé?"

deep.x: The name evokes a scarecrow: a fake opponent stuffed with straw, easy to knock down. You "win" a fight with someone who isn't there.
How it's built

x: **Exaggeration**: "lower speed limits near schools" becomes "ban cars"
**Oversimplification**: dropping the conditions and qualifiers
**Cherry-picking**: quoting the weakest supporter, not the best
**Weak man**: attacking a real but feeble version while ignoring stronger ones

deep.x: Why it's so common
It works on audiences who haven't heard the original view. It's also easy to do by accident: we remember opponents' views in their simplest form. News headlines and short videos make it easier still.
How to defend yourself
Restate your view calmly: "That's not what I said. I said X, under conditions Y." Ask the other person to put your view in their own words before arguing.

x: Claim: "We should tax sugary drinks"
Straw man: "So you want to ban treats"
Fair version: "You think a price signal will cut sugar intake"
Now real debate: does it work, and is it fair?

deep.x: Several European countries, Portugal among them since 2017, have introduced taxes on sugary drinks, so this debate is a real one, not just a textbook case.
Before you refute a view, make sure it's the view the other person actually holds.

cards.title: Falso dilema

items.r: Que outras opções existem?

cards.text: Apresentar só duas opções quando existem mais. "Ou você está com a gente ou contra a gente" ignora as muitas posições intermediárias.

deep.x: Also called false dichotomy or black-and-white thinking. It frames a choice as having only two options when there are more, so rejecting one seems to force you into the other.
Why it persuades
Two options feel simple. If one is plainly terrible, the other looks good by contrast, without being examined. Campaigns, adverts and heated debates use it constantly, across the political spectrum.
Common forms

x: Either/or: "Either we cut taxes or the economy collapses"
Perfect or nothing: "If it doesn't solve everything, it's useless"
Two causes only: "It's either genetic or it's upbringing" (usually both interact)

deep.x: When two options are real
Some choices really are binary: a light switch is on or off; you either take the flight or you don't. The fallacy is not having two options, but claiming there are only two without showing it.

x: "Either we build the new motorway or the town dies"
Ask: what else is possible?
Rail link, better buses, remote work, upgrade old road
At least four more options to compare

deep.x: When someone offers only two choices, ask what the third one is.

cards.title: Ladeira escorregadia

steps: Desastre, sem provas para cada elo

cards.text: Afirmar que um pequeno passo vai levar inevitavelmente a um desastre, sem mostrar por quê. Às vezes a ladeira é real; a falácia está em supô-la.

deep.x: The argument says: if we allow A, then B will follow, then C, and soon catastrophe Z. The fallacy lies in asserting each step without evidence that it will actually happen.
Do the maths
Even if each step is fairly likely, a long chain becomes unlikely, because the probabilities multiply.

x: 4 steps, each 80% likely
Whole chain only about 41% likely
With 6 steps: about 26%

v.unit: % chance whole chain happens (80% per step)

deep.x: When slopes are real

Some slopes do exist. Precedents in law make later steps easier. Small dishonesties can grow into habits. A good slippery-slope argument shows the **mechanism** pushing each step: legal precedent, financial incentive, psychological habit, and gives evidence for it.

x: Weak: "If we allow this, anything goes"
Stronger: "This ruling sets a precedent courts have extended in three similar cases"

deep.x: Not just "slopes"

A cousin is the "line-drawing" worry: if we can't say exactly where to stop, we'll never stop. But we draw lines all the time, like the speed limit and the voting age, even when the exact number is partly arbitrary.

deep.w: Every slippery-slope argument is a fallacy
deep.r: It's only fallacious when the steps are assumed; with evidence for each link, it can be strong

deep.x: For a slope to be slippery, someone has to show why each step leads to the next.

cards.title: Apelo à popularidade

items.r: Quais são as provas?

cards.text: "Milhões de pessoas acreditam nisso, então deve ser verdade." Popularidade não é prova; muitas crenças populares se revelaram falsas.

deep.x: Latin name: **argumentum ad populum**, the appeal to the people. Also called the bandwagon fallacy. It treats how many believe something as proof that it's true.
Popular and false

x: Most educated Europeans once believed the Sun orbits the Earth
Many people still believe we use only 10% of our brains (we use virtually all of it)
Many think the Great Wall of China is visible from the Moon with the naked eye (it isn't)

deep.x: Why we fall for it

In the 1950s, psychologist Solomon Asch asked people to match line lengths after actors gave obviously wrong answers. About three quarters of participants went along with the wrong answer at least once. Belonging feels good; standing out feels risky.
When numbers do count

Sometimes popularity is evidence. A busy restaurant probably isn't terrible. Independent guesses can be surprisingly accurate: at a 1906 English fair, the median of about 800 guesses of an ox's weight was within about 1% of the real figure. The key is **independence**: crowds are wise when people judge separately, not when they copy each other.

deep.w: If experts agree, that's just popularity too
deep.r: A consensus of experts who've checked the evidence is good evidence; it's a crowd of specialists judging independently

deep.x: How many people believe something tells you little; why they believe it tells you much more.

cards.title: Correlação vs. causalidade
cards.text: As vendas de sorvete e os afogamentos sobem juntos, mas sorvete não causa afogamento: o calor faz os dois subirem. Uma ligação não prova que uma coisa causa a outra.

deep.x: When two things move together, it's tempting to conclude one causes the other. But there are several other explanations to rule out first.
The four suspects

x: **Confounder**: hot weather drives both ice cream sales and swimming (and so drownings)
**Reverse causation**: do people get sick because they're in hospital, or go to hospital because they're sick?
**Coincidence**: with enough data, unrelated trends will line up by chance
**Real cause**: sometimes A really does cause B, but you need more evidence to show it

deep.x: Post hoc
A close cousin is **post hoc ergo propter hoc**: "after this, therefore because of this". "I wore my lucky scarf and Benfica won." The order of events alone proves nothing.

x: Towns with more fire engines have more fire damage
Do fire engines cause damage?
Confounder: bigger towns have more fires and more engines
Compare towns of the same size instead

deep.x: The website "Spurious Correlations" shows absurd matches, such as the number of films Nicolas Cage appeared in tracking swimming-pool drownings in the US for several years.
When two things rise together, look for the hidden third thing before blaming either.

cards.title: Steelmanning
cards.text: O contrário do espantalho: apresente a posição do seu oponente na forma mais forte antes de responder. Se ele disser "sim, é exatamente isso que eu penso", você está pronto para discordar.

deep.x: The term is a play on "straw man": instead of building a weak version of your opponent, build the strongest one, made of steel. Philosophers call the underlying idea the **principle of charity**.
Rapoport's rules
Philosopher Daniel Dennett popularised a set of rules, credited to the game theorist Anatol Rapoport, for criticising a view fairly.
Why it works

x: You might discover they're right, or partly right
If you refute the strongest version, the weaker ones fall too
People listen to someone who has clearly listened to them
It protects you from defeating a view nobody holds

deep.x: An old idea

John Stuart Mill argued in *On Liberty* (1859) that someone who knows only their own side of a question hardly knows even that. Ancient Indian and medieval Islamic debate traditions required stating the opponent's position (**pūrvapakṣa** in Sanskrit) before responding.

x: View: "We should raise the minimum wage"
Your steel man of opposition: "It may cut hiring for the least experienced workers"
Their steel man of yours: "It lifts pay for millions with modest job effects"
Now discuss the evidence

deep.x: Argue with the best version of a view, or you haven't really argued with it at all.

quiz.q: "Você não pode confiar no argumento dela, ela não é especialista." Que falácia é essa?
quiz.explain: Ataca a pessoa, não o argumento.

quiz.q: As vendas de sorvete e os afogamentos aumentam no verão. Isso mostra…
quiz.explain: O calor faz os dois subirem.

cards.title: O estado de natureza
cards.text: Os filósofos imaginaram a vida sem nenhum governo para perguntar por que aceitamos governantes. As respostas deles moldaram as democracias modernas.

deep.x: Social contract philosophers asked you to imagine humans living with no government, laws or police. This wasn't meant as history. It was a thought experiment: by picturing life without the state, we can ask what the state is for and when it is legitimate.
The social contract

The common move: free, equal individuals agree to give up some freedom to a government in exchange for something better, such as security, rights or a common good. Legitimate power rests on the consent of the governed, not on divine right or conquest.
The objections

x: **Hume** (1748) noted no one actually signed. Saying you consent by staying is like saying a sailor, carried aboard asleep, consents to the captain because he doesn't jump overboard
**Historians and anthropologists** note humans always lived in groups with rules, never as isolated individuals
**Feminist critics** such as Carole Pateman (1988) argued the classic contracts assumed men as the parties and left women's subordination unexamined

deep.x: The idea of consent behind rulers echoes in many modern constitutions, including Portugal's, which says sovereignty "resides in the people".
Imagining life without government is a way of asking what government owes us.

cards.title: O Leviatã de Hobbes
cards.text: Thomas Hobbes (1651) defendeu que, sem um soberano poderoso, as pessoas viveriam em uma guerra de todos contra todos. Trocamos liberdade por segurança.

deep.x: Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) lived through the English Civil War (1642–1651), in which perhaps a few per cent of the population died. *Leviathan*, published in 1651, is a book shaped by that terror of collapse.
The war of all against all

Without a common power to keep everyone in awe, Hobbes argued, people roughly equal in strength, competing for scarce goods and fearful of each other, would strike first. No farming, no trade, no arts, and life would be solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short.
The sovereign

To escape, everyone transfers their right of self-rule to one sovereign power, a person or assembly, with near-absolute authority. Rebellion is almost never allowed, because any return to chaos is worse than a bad ruler. But Hobbes kept one exception: you may resist if the sovereign tries to kill you.
Objections

John Locke mocked the idea that people would escape the danger of foxes by giving all power to a lion. If the sovereign is unchecked, who protects you from the sovereign? Hobbes's defenders reply that he showed why order matters and why failed states are so deadly.
The book's famous frontispiece shows a giant crowned figure whose body is made of hundreds of tiny people: the state as an artificial person made of its citizens.
Hobbes's fear was simple: without someone in charge, everyone loses.

cards.title: Locke e os direitos

items: Direito de trocar um mau governo

cards.text: John Locke defendeu que as pessoas têm direitos naturais à vida, à liberdade e à propriedade, e que um governo que os viole pode ser substituído. Ele influenciou os fundadores dos EUA.
