cards.text: Agostinho de Hipona (354–430) uniu a fé cristã às ideias de Platão. Suas *Confissões* são uma das primeiras grandes autobiografias e exploram a memória, o tempo e o eu.

deep.x: Augustine was born in 354 in Thagaste, a Roman town in what is now Algeria, to a pagan father and a devout Christian mother, Monica. He trained as a teacher of rhetoric and spent years searching: first in Manichaeism, a religion that saw the world as a battle between good and evil powers, then in the Neoplatonism of Plotinus.
Why the Confessions is new

The *Confessions* (about 397–400) is written as a long prayer addressed to God. Augustine looks back at his own restless desires, from stealing pears as a boy "for the thrill of it" to his famous conversion in a Milan garden in 386. No earlier author had examined his inner life in such detail. The book is less a list of events than an investigation of what a self is.
Memory and time

In Book 10 he marvels at memory as a vast inner palace, holding things he is not thinking of right now. In Book 11 he asks what time is, and admits he knows until someone asks him to explain it. His answer: time lives in the mind as a stretching of the soul.
After Rome was sacked in 410, he wrote *The City of God*, contrasting the earthly city, built on love of self, with the heavenly city, built on love of God.
Augustine turned philosophy inwards: to find truth, he said, look within yourself.
Augustine anticipated Descartes by about 1,200 years: he argued that even if he is deceived, he must exist in order to be deceived.

cards.title: O problema do mal
cards.text: Se Deus é onipotente e sumamente bom, por que o mal existe? Agostinho respondeu que o mal é uma ausência de bem, causada em parte pelo livre-arbítrio humano.

deep.x: The problem is old. A version usually credited to Epicurus runs: if God wants to stop evil but can't, he isn't all-powerful; if he can but won't, he isn't all-good. So why is there evil? This is called the **logical problem of evil**: it claims God and evil cannot both exist.
Augustine's two answers

First, evil is not a thing that God created. It is a **privation**, an absence of good, the way blindness is an absence of sight or rot is a lack of soundness in wood. Second, moral evil comes from free creatures who turn away from the higher good towards lesser goods. A world with free beings who can choose love is, he argued, better than a world of puppets.
Later replies and objections

Critics raise strong objections. Calling evil an "absence" does not make a child's pain hurt any less. Free will may explain cruelty, but what about **natural evil**: earthquakes, plagues, cancer? The 1755 Lisbon earthquake, which killed tens of thousands on All Saints' Day, made many Europeans ask exactly this. Modern philosophers often shift to the **evidential problem**: even if God and evil are logically compatible, does the sheer amount of suffering make God unlikely?
The problem of evil is the most discussed challenge to belief in God, and the answers remain contested on both sides.
Alvin Plantinga's 1974 free will defence persuaded many philosophers, including some atheists, that the purely logical version fails, so debate has largely moved to the evidential one.

cards.title: Boécio
cards.text: Na prisão, aguardando a execução em 524, Boécio escreveu *A Consolação da Filosofia*: a Senhora Filosofia ensina que a verdadeira felicidade não pode ser tirada pela fortuna.

deep.x: Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524) was a Roman aristocrat serving Theodoric, the Ostrogothic king who ruled Italy. He reached the top: consul in 510, and later head of the civil service. Then he was accused of treason, imprisoned near Pavia, and executed.
A book written on death row

*The Consolation of Philosophy* alternates prose with poems. Boethius, bitter and self-pitying, is visited by Lady Philosophy, a tall woman whose dress is torn by rival schools that each ripped off a piece. She shows him that Fortune's gifts were never truly his: Fortune is a wheel, and turning is its nature.
False goods and the true good
Lady Philosophy goes through what people chase and shows that each falls short.

True happiness, she argues, is the highest good itself, which is God, and it cannot be taken away. In the final book Boethius tackles a puzzle: if God knows what I will do, am I free? His answer is that God is outside time and sees all moments in one eternal present, as you might watch someone walk without forcing their steps.

deep.w: Boethius was just a gloomy prisoner
deep.r: He was a major scholar who translated Aristotle's logic into Latin, Europe's main source for it for 600 years

deep.x: What fortune gives, fortune can take; only what is within you is truly yours.
The Consolation was one of the most-read books of the Middle Ages: King Alfred, Chaucer and Queen Elizabeth I all translated it.

cards.title: A era de ouro islâmica
cards.text: Estudiosos como Avicena (Ibn Sina) e Averróis (Ibn Rushd) preservaram e desenvolveram a filosofia grega. Seus comentários sobre Aristóteles moldaram o pensamento europeu.

deep.x: From the late 700s, the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad paid scholars to translate Greek science and philosophy into Arabic. Many translators were Christians who worked from Greek and Syriac. The result was a library of Aristotle, Plato's ideas, Galen and Euclid in Arabic.
Not just preserving
Philosophers in the Islamic world (*falsafa*) built new systems on this base. They asked how Greek reason fitted with the Qur'an, how the soul relates to the body, and what makes something necessary.
A famous debate

Around 1095 the theologian al-Ghazali wrote *The Incoherence of the Philosophers*, arguing that some of their claims, such as the eternity of the world, were unproven and against faith. About 80 years later Averroes, a judge in Córdoba, replied with *The Incoherence of the Incoherence*, defending philosophy. The exchange is still read as a classic of faith-and-reason debate.
How it reached Europe

In the 1100s, translators in Toledo, such as Gerard of Cremona, turned Arabic works into Latin. Medieval Latin writers simply called Aristotle "the Philosopher" and Averroes "the Commentator". Avicenna's *Canon of Medicine* was taught in European medical schools for about 500 years.

deep.w: Muslim scholars only kept Greek books safe
deep.r: They added original ideas in logic, medicine, optics and metaphysics that Europe then studied

deep.x: Much of what medieval Europe knew of Aristotle arrived through Arabic, carrying Islamic thinkers' ideas with it.
What is now southern Portugal was part of al-Andalus for about 500 years; Silves was a lively centre of Arabic poetry and learning.

cards.title: O homem suspenso de Avicena

steps: O eu não é o corpo?

cards.text: Avicena imaginou um homem criado flutuando no ar, de olhos vendados, sem tocar em nada. Mesmo assim, ele saberia que existe: consciência de si sem os sentidos.

deep.x: Ibn Sina (980–1037), known in Latin as Avicenna, was a Persian polymath who wrote on medicine, logic and metaphysics. In his work on the soul, part of the huge *Book of the Cure*, he set out a thought experiment that later readers called the "floating man".
The set-up

Imagine you are created in an instant, already adult, suspended in air so still that you feel no breeze. Your limbs are spread so they do not touch each other. You have never had any sensations. Would you know that you exist? Avicenna says yes, at once. Yet you would not know that you have a body, hands or a heart.
What he concluded

If you can know your self while knowing nothing of your body, then the self is not the same thing as the body. For Avicenna this pointed to an immaterial soul. He also used it to show that self-awareness is the most basic kind of knowledge, prior to learning anything through the senses.
Objections

x: Imagining something is not proof it is possible: can a never-stimulated brain even think?
Knowing X without knowing Y doesn't show X and Y differ. Someone can know Lisbon without knowing it is Portugal's largest city.
Modern neuroscience suggests our sense of self is built from body signals, including the inner sense of where our limbs are.

deep.w: Descartes invented the "I exist" argument from nothing
deep.r: Avicenna made a similar move about 600 years earlier, and Latin scholars read him

deep.x: The floating man asks what you would still know about yourself if every sense were switched off.

cards.title: Maimônides
cards.text: Moisés Maimônides, filósofo judeu nascido em Córdoba, buscou conciliar a fé com a razão de Aristóteles em seu *Guia dos Perplexos*.

deep.x: Moses ben Maimon (c. 1138–1204), known as Maimonides or by the acronym Rambam, was born in Córdoba in Muslim Spain. When the strict Almohad rulers took power, Jews were pressed to convert, and his family fled. After years in Fez, he settled in Egypt, where he became a court physician and leader of the Jewish community.
Who was perplexed?

He wrote the *Guide for the Perplexed* in Arabic, in Hebrew letters, for an educated Jew who had studied Aristotle and was troubled that Scripture seemed to clash with philosophy. His approach: when the Bible talks of God's hand or anger, read it as metaphor. Reason and revelation, properly read, agree.
Speaking about God by negation
Maimonides held that God is so far beyond us that positive statements mislead. We can only say what God is not. Each denial removes an error and brings us closer.
Where reason stops

Aristotle taught that the world is eternal. Maimonides argued neither eternity nor creation can be strictly proved. Since reason cannot decide, he accepted creation, as Scripture teaches. This careful line, giving reason its due but naming its limits, influenced Thomas Aquinas, who cites "Rabbi Moses".

deep.w: Medieval religious thinkers simply rejected reason
deep.r: Maimonides treated rational study as a religious duty

deep.x: Maimonides argued that faith understood through reason is deeper than faith without it.
His *Guide* was so controversial that some Jewish scholars opposed it, and copies were burned in Montpellier in 1232.

cards.title: Tomás de Aquino
cards.text: Tomás de Aquino (1225–1274) combinou Aristóteles com a teologia cristã, defendendo que a fé e a razão não podem estar realmente em conflito porque ambas vêm de Deus.

deep.x: Thomas Aquinas was born around 1225 near Aquino, in southern Italy, into a noble family. When he chose to join the new Dominican order of wandering preachers, his brothers kidnapped him and held him at home for about a year. He escaped, studied under Albert the Great, and became a master at the University of Paris.
Two roads to one truth

Aquinas held that some truths can be reached by reason, and others only through revelation. Because both come from God, a real conflict is impossible. If philosophy seems to contradict faith, there is a mistake in the reasoning, and better reasoning will find it. This let him use Aristotle, a pagan, as a serious guide.
Big ideas

x: **Natural law**: basic moral rules, such as preserving life, can be known by reason by anyone.
**Just war**: war needs proper authority, a just cause and right intention.
**The Summa Theologiae**: a vast, unfinished guide to theology, written as thousands of questions.

deep.x: Not always welcome

In 1277 the Bishop of Paris condemned 219 propositions linked to Aristotle's influence, and some matched Aquinas's views. Only later did he become the Catholic Church's model theologian: he was made a saint in 1323. Critics, from Protestant reformers to modern sceptics, question whether reason can really go as far towards God as he thought.
For Aquinas, faith and reason are like two windows looking onto the same landscape.
Classmates nicknamed the large, quiet Thomas "the dumb ox"; Albert reportedly replied that this ox's bellowing would be heard around the world.

cards.title: As cinco vias
cards.text: Tomás de Aquino apresentou cinco argumentos para a existência de Deus, entre eles o do "primeiro motor": tudo o que se move é movido por algo, então precisa haver um primeiro motor imóvel.

deep.x: In his *Summa Theologiae* Aquinas gives five short arguments that God exists. Each starts from something we observe and reasons back to its source. They take up barely a page.
The first way, step by step

Things change: a log becomes hot because fire heats it. Nothing changes itself from potential to actual; something already actual must do it. If each mover is itself moved by another, without a first, nothing would move at all. So there must be a first, unmoved mover, "and this everyone understands to be God".
A common misreading

items.w: First in time: a Big Bang starter
items.r: First in order: what holds change up now

deep.x: Aquinas actually thought reason could not prove the universe had a beginning. His chain is like a hanging lamp: the chain only works if something holds the top right now.
Objections

x: Why can't the chain go on for ever? Defenders say an infinite chain of borrowed motion explains nothing; critics reply there's no contradiction in it.
Even if there is a first cause, why think it is personal, good or the God of any religion?
Hume and Kant doubted that cause-and-effect reasoning applies beyond experience.
The fifth way, from order, was weakened in many eyes by Darwin's explanation of design-like features.

deep.x: The five ways ask why there is change and order at all, not just how they began.

deep.w: "Who moved the first mover?" defeats the argument
deep.r: The argument claims the first mover is not the kind of thing that needs moving, so the real debate is whether that idea makes sense

cards.title: A navalha de Ockham

items.r: Usar só o necessário

cards.text: Guilherme de Ockham (c. 1287–1347) defendeu que não devemos multiplicar entidades além do necessário. Seu princípio se tornou a famosa "navalha".

deep.x: William of Ockham was an English Franciscan friar, born around 1287 in the village of Ockham in Surrey. He studied at Oxford, was summoned to the papal court at Avignon to answer charges about his teaching, and in 1328 fled to the protection of Emperor Louis of Bavaria. He died in Munich around 1347, possibly from the Black Death.
What he actually said

The famous wording, "entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity", doesn't appear in his writings. He wrote similar things, such as "plurality should not be posited without necessity". The name "razor" came much later: it shaves off unneeded assumptions.
Why he used it

Ockham was a **nominalist**: he argued that "redness" or "humanity" are not real things floating apart from individual red objects or individual people. They are names and concepts in our minds. Why posit extra entities when individuals explain everything?
The razor today

Scientists and doctors use a version of it: prefer the explanation that needs fewer assumptions. A doctor hearing hooves thinks horses, not zebras. Software engineers favour the simplest design that works.

items.r: Prefer it until evidence demands more

deep.w: Ockham's razor proves the simplest answer is right
deep.r: It's a rule of thumb for choosing what to test first, not proof; nature is sometimes complicated

deep.x: Don't add assumptions you don't need, but don't remove ones the evidence requires.
Ockham was excommunicated after his flight from Avignon; his razor was partly a weapon for cutting back what he saw as needless theological speculation.

cards.title: Universidades
cards.text: A Europa medieval fundou universidades, entre elas a de Coimbra, em 1290, uma das mais antigas do mundo em funcionamento contínuo. A filosofia e a teologia estavam no centro delas.

deep.x: The word *universitas* simply meant a guild or corporation: a self-governing body of teachers or students, like a guild of bakers. Bologna (from about 1088) and Paris (late 1100s) were the models. Students paid masters, elected officers and could go on strike or move away.
Portugal's university

King Dinis founded a "General Study" in Lisbon in 1290, confirmed by the Pope the same year. It moved back and forth between Lisbon and Coimbra several times before settling in Coimbra for good in 1537 under João III. Today the University of Coimbra is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
What students learned

Arts students started young, around 14, with the seven liberal arts. Only after years of logic and philosophy could they enter the higher faculties. Theology took the longest, often more than a decade.
Learning by arguing

Teaching was built on the **disputation**: a question was posed, arguments on each side were set out, a master gave an answer, and every objection was answered. This "scholastic method" trained people to state opposing views fairly before rejecting them.

deep.w: Medieval universities just repeated Church dogma
deep.r: Disputation required arguing both sides, and masters disagreed fiercely, sometimes with official condemnations

deep.x: The university, with its degrees, faculties and debates, is one of the Middle Ages' most lasting inventions.
Coimbra's 18th-century Joanina Library is guarded by a colony of small bats that eat book-damaging insects at night.

quiz.q: Quem escreveu A Consolação da Filosofia na prisão?
O que Tomás de Aquino pensava sobre a fé e a razão?
options: Não podem estar realmente em conflito

quiz.q: Quando foi fundada a primeira universidade de Portugal?
quiz.explain: Em Lisboa, depois transferida para Coimbra.

cards.title: Ouse saber
cards.text: Em 1784, Kant definiu o Iluminismo como a saída da humanidade da menoridade pela qual ela própria é culpada. Seu lema: *Sapere aude*, ouse pensar por si mesmo.

deep.x: In 1783 a Berlin magazine asked, in a footnote, "What is enlightenment?" Kant answered in December 1784 with a short essay. Enlightenment, he said, is leaving behind an **immaturity** that is self-inflicted: not a lack of intelligence, but a lack of courage to use it without someone else's guidance.
Why we stay immature

Kant blamed laziness and fear. It's comfortable to have a book think for you, a pastor be your conscience and a doctor decide your diet. Guardians, meanwhile, warn us that independent thinking is dangerous. The motto *Sapere aude*, "dare to be wise", comes from the Roman poet Horace.
Public and private reason

Kant's surprising distinction: an officer must obey orders on duty (the "private" use of reason, in a post). But as a scholar writing for the public, the same officer may freely criticise military policy.

He wrote under the Prussian king Frederick the Great, whose attitude he summed up as: argue as much as you like, but obey. Kant added that his was not yet an enlightened age, only an age of enlightenment: the process was still going on.
Later critics

x: Hamann, Kant's friend, said "immaturity" was easy to blame on others while the guardians stayed in charge.
In 1944, Adorno and Horkheimer argued that Enlightenment reason can turn into a tool of domination.
Michel Foucault, in 1984, recast it as a permanent attitude of questioning, not a finished project.

deep.x: Enlightenment, for Kant, is not knowing more but daring to think for yourself.
The same year, Moses Mendelssohn published his own answer to the question in the same Berlin magazine.

cards.title: Espinosa
cards.text: Baruch Espinosa, de ascendência judaico-portuguesa, identificou Deus com a própria Natureza e defendeu a liberdade de pensamento. Foi expulso da comunidade judaica de Amsterdã em 1656.

deep.x: Baruch (or Bento) de Spinoza was born in Amsterdam in 1632 to a family of Portuguese Jews who had fled the Inquisition. His father, Miguel, was a merchant born in Portugal. The community spoke Portuguese and Spanish; Spinoza grew up between Dutch, Portuguese and Hebrew.
Expelled at 23

In July 1656, the Amsterdam synagogue issued an unusually harsh *herem*, a ban, cursing him and forbidding members to speak with him. The text does not specify his "abominable heresies", but they likely included denying an immortal soul and a personal God. He earned his living grinding lenses.
God or Nature

In the *Ethics*, written like a geometry book with definitions and proofs, Spinoza argues there is only one substance, which he calls "God, or Nature". Mind and body are not two things but two ways of seeing the same reality.
Freedom, for Spinoza, is not escaping causes but understanding them. The more we grasp why we feel what we feel, the less our passions push us around.
Freedom of thought

His *Theological-Political Treatise* (1670), published anonymously, argued that the Bible should be studied like any historical text, and that a state is safest when people may think and say what they like.

deep.w: Spinoza was simply an atheist
deep.r: Some readers saw him as an atheist, others as "God-intoxicated"; the label depends on what you mean by God

deep.x: Spinoza made God and Nature one, and found freedom in understanding why things happen.
In 1929 Einstein said he believed in "Spinoza's God", one who shows himself in the order of the world, not one who concerns himself with human fates.

cards.title: Voltaire
cards.text: Voltaire atacou a intolerância e a perseguição religiosa com humor. O terremoto de Lisboa de 1755 inspirou seu *Cândido*, que zomba da ideia de que este é o "melhor dos mundos possíveis".

deep.x: Voltaire was the pen name of François-Marie Arouet (1694–1778). His wit got him locked in the Bastille twice. Exiled to England in 1726, he admired its relative freedom of religion and the press, and Newton's science, and praised them in his *Letters on the English*.
Lisbon, 1 November 1755
On All Saints' Day morning a huge earthquake, followed by a tsunami and fires, destroyed much of Lisbon. Tens of thousands died. People across Europe asked how a good God could allow it.
Candide

Leibniz had argued that God, being perfect, must have created the best of all possible worlds. In *Candide* (1759), the tutor Pangloss repeats that "all is for the best" while being hanged, flogged and enslaved, and while Lisbon shakes around him. The book ends with the advice that "we must cultivate our garden": work at what's in front of you.
Against intolerance

In 1762 Jean Calas, a Protestant in Toulouse, was tortured and executed on a false charge of killing his son to stop him converting. Voltaire campaigned for three years until Calas was cleared, and wrote his *Treatise on Tolerance*.
Critics note the caricature: Leibniz didn't deny suffering; he claimed any other world would be worse overall. Rousseau also replied that people, not nature, had packed Lisbon into tall buildings.

deep.w: Voltaire said "I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it"
deep.r: An English writer, Evelyn Beatrice Hall, wrote that line in 1906 to sum up his attitude

deep.x: Voltaire used laughter as a weapon against cruelty and comfortable excuses.

cards.title: O ceticismo de Hume

items: O eu é um feixe de percepções

cards.text: David Hume duvidava que pudéssemos conhecer com certeza as causas, o eu ou os milagres. Kant disse que Hume o despertou do seu "sono dogmático".

deep.x: David Hume (1711–1776), from Edinburgh, wrote *A Treatise of Human Nature* in his twenties. He later said it "fell dead-born from the press". Suspected of atheism, he was twice turned down for university posts, yet became famous as a historian.
Do we ever see a cause?

Watch one billiard ball hit another. You see ball A move, contact, ball B move. You never see a "force" or "necessary connection" passing between them. After many repetitions, your mind simply comes to expect B to move.

This leads to the **problem of induction**: we assume the future will be like the past, but we can't prove that without assuming it again. The sun has risen every day; logic alone can't guarantee tomorrow.
Three targets

Look inside for your "self", Hume said, and you only ever find a perception: heat, a thought, a feeling. On miracles, he argued we should believe a report only if its being false would be even more miraculous than the event.
Is he right?

Critics reply that if Hume's doubts were true, science would be impossible; defenders say science works on well-grounded habits, not certainty. Thomas Reid argued we are entitled to trust common sense. Many think the problem of induction is still unsolved.

deep.w: A sceptic thinks nothing is true
deep.r: Hume lived by habit and common sense; he only doubted that reason could prove what we instinctively believe

deep.x: Hume showed that much of what we call knowledge rests on habit, not proof.
Hume also argued you can't derive an "ought" from an "is": facts alone don't tell you what to do.

cards.title: A síntese de Kant
cards.text: Kant defendeu que a mente estrutura ativamente a experiência com o espaço, o tempo e a causalidade. Conhecemos as coisas como elas aparecem para nós, não como são em si mesmas.

deep.x: In 1781 Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) published the *Critique of Pure Reason*. He was trying to settle a long fight between two camps about where knowledge comes from.
The Copernican turn

Copernicus explained the sky's motion by moving the observer. Kant did the same for knowledge. Instead of our minds conforming to objects, objects as we experience them conform to our mind's structure. The mind is not a blank screen but an active organiser.

Space and time are the "forms" of our senses. Concepts such as cause and effect are rules the understanding applies. So Hume was right that we never see causation in the raw, but wrong to think it is merely habit: it is a condition of any experience at all. In his short phrase, thoughts without content are empty, intuitions without concepts are blind.
Two sides of things

x: **Phenomena**: things as they appear to us, which science can know in great detail.
**Things in themselves**: what reality is like apart from our minds, which we can never know.

deep.x: Objections

Non-Euclidean geometry and Einstein's relativity challenged Kant's claim that the geometry of space is fixed by our minds. Others asked how he can say anything about things in themselves, even that they exist and cause our sensations.

deep.w: Kant said the outside world isn't real
deep.r: He said it is real, but we know it only as it appears through our own forms of experience

deep.x: We don't see the world as it is; we see it as minds like ours must see it.
Kant never travelled more than about 150 km from Königsberg, and neighbours were said to set their watches by his afternoon walk.

cards.title: A Encyclopédie
cards.text: A *Encyclopédie* de Diderot e d'Alembert (1751–1772) reuniu o conhecimento humano, incluindo ofícios e ciências, para difundir a razão amplamente.

deep.x: The project began modestly in 1745 as a French translation of Ephraim Chambers' English *Cyclopaedia*. Under Denis Diderot and the mathematician Jean d'Alembert it became something far bigger: a full survey of human knowledge.
A map of knowledge
D'Alembert's preface sorted knowledge by mental faculty, following Francis Bacon. Notably, theology was placed as one branch of philosophy, not at the top.
Crafts deserve respect

Diderot visited workshops to describe how stockings, glass and paper were made. Thousands of engravings showed tools and trades in detail. The message: practical skill is knowledge too, and spreading it improves lives.
Battles with censors

Articles slipped criticism into unlikely places, and cross-references led readers from dull entries to sharp ones. In 1759 the government revoked its licence and the Pope condemned it. D'Alembert stepped back, and Diderot finished the text volumes largely in secret.

deep.w: Diderot wrote the Encyclopédie
deep.r: Over 140 people contributed; the Chevalier de Jaucourt alone wrote about a quarter of the articles

deep.x: The Encyclopédie aimed to change how people think by giving everyone access to how things work.
Diderot discovered in 1764 that his own printer had secretly cut passages he thought too dangerous, after the proofs were approved.

cards.title: Wollstonecraft
cards.text: Em *Reivindicação dos Direitos da Mulher* (1792), Mary Wollstonecraft defendeu que as mulheres só parecem inferiores porque a educação lhes é negada.

deep.x: Mary Wollstonecraft (1759–1797) grew up in a household with a violent, debt-ridden father. She worked as a companion, a governess and a teacher, then as a writer and translator in London, unusual for a woman then.
The argument

In *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman* (1792), she replied to writers like Rousseau, who held that girls should be educated only to please men. If women seemed vain or weak, she argued, that was the product of training, not nature.

Her claim rests on Enlightenment logic: if rights come from reason, and women have reason, then women have the same rights. She called for girls and boys to be taught together, for women to be able to earn their own living, and for marriage to be a partnership of equals.
Limits and legacy

Later feminists noted that she still assumed most women would be mothers at home, and wrote mainly about the middle class. Her reputation suffered when her husband William Godwin published a frank memoir of her love affairs. In the 20th century she was rediscovered as a founder of modern feminism.

deep.w: She argued women were already equal in practice
deep.r: She argued they were equal in reason but kept unequal by education and law

deep.x: Wollstonecraft's point: you can't judge what someone is capable of after denying them the means to develop it.
In 1785 she travelled to Lisbon to nurse her closest friend, Fanny Blood, in childbirth; Fanny died there. Wollstonecraft later died after giving birth to Mary Shelley, author of *Frankenstein*.

cards.title: Adam Smith
cards.text: Adam Smith, filósofo moral, defendeu em 1776 que o interesse próprio em mercados livres pode beneficiar a sociedade, como uma "mão invisível". Ele também escreveu sobre a simpatia e a ética.

deep.x: Adam Smith (1723–1790) was professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow. His first book, *The Theory of Moral Sentiments* (1759), was about ethics. He saw it as just as important as *The Wealth of Nations* (1776).
Self-interest and markets

Smith's famous point: we don't get our dinner from the butcher, brewer or baker's kindness, but from their own interest. In a competitive market, people pursuing their own gain are led, "as by an invisible hand", to serve others' needs too.
The pin factory

items.l: pins a day for one alone

deep.x: Dividing work into small steps multiplies output. But Smith warned that endless repetition can make workers "stupid and ignorant", and so he supported public education.
Not a simple free-marketeer

x: He warned that business owners rarely meet even for fun without conspiring against the public.
He backed some rules, like on banking, and public works.
His ethics rests on **sympathy**: imagining ourselves in another's place, judged by an inner "impartial spectator".

deep.x: He criticised the 1703 Methuen Treaty between Portugal and Britain (port wine for English cloth) as an example of special trade favours. Economists still argue about how far markets need rules, and both sides cite Smith.

deep.w: The invisible hand is the core of Smith's book
deep.r: The phrase appears only once in The Wealth of Nations

deep.x: Smith thought markets can turn self-interest to public good, but only within a society of laws, morals and fellow-feeling.

cards.title: Revoluções
cards.text: As ideias iluministas sobre os direitos e o consentimento dos governados alimentaram a Revolução Americana (1776) e a Revolução Francesa (1789).

deep.x: Enlightenment thinkers didn't plan revolutions, but they supplied the vocabulary. John Locke (1689) argued people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and governments exist by consent to protect them. A government that violates them may be resisted.
America, 1776

The Declaration of Independence asserts that people have unalienable rights and that governments derive "their just powers from the consent of the governed". The US Constitution of 1787 divided power between legislature, executive and courts, as Montesquieu recommended.
France, 1789
The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (August 1789) proclaimed that people are born free and equal in rights, and that sovereignty lies in the nation.
Hard questions

x: Rights were proclaimed while slavery continued and women were excluded; Haiti's enslaved people took the promise literally.
Edmund Burke (1790) warned that tearing down traditions would end in violence; the Terror seemed to some to confirm this.
Others reply that the violence came from war and crisis, not from the ideas of rights themselves.

deep.x: Portugal's Liberal Revolution began in Porto on 24 August 1820, leading to the country's first constitution in 1822.
Revolutions turned Enlightenment ideas of rights and consent into documents that still shape constitutions, including Portugal's.

cards.title: As reformas de Pombal
cards.text: Em Portugal, o Marquês de Pombal reconstruiu Lisboa e impulsionou reformas de inspiração iluminista: modernizou a Universidade de Coimbra, o ensino laico e a ciência, embora governasse com mão de ferro.

deep.x: Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo (1699–1782) became King José I's chief minister in 1750 and dominated government for 27 years. He was made Marquis of Pombal in 1769. He had served as a diplomat in London and Vienna, where he saw how other states were modernising.
Rebuilding Lisbon

After the 1755 earthquake he organised the response: burying the dead, preventing looting, controlling prices. The Baixa was rebuilt on a strict grid with wide streets. Buildings used the **gaiola pombalina**, a flexible wooden cage inside the walls to resist shaking. Officials sent every parish a questionnaire about the quake, which is often called a founding moment of modern seismology.
Reforms

The 1772 Coimbra reform added faculties of mathematics and natural philosophy, a botanical garden, a chemistry lab and an observatory. In 1756 he created one of the world's first demarcated wine regions, in the Douro.
The iron hand

Pombal was an **enlightened despot**: modern goals, absolute methods. After an attempt on the king's life in 1758, members of the powerful Távora family were publicly executed in 1759, after a trial many historians consider unjust. He expelled the Jesuits, censored opponents and filled prisons. When Queen Maria I took the throne in 1777, he was dismissed and many prisoners were freed.
Pombal shows the Enlightenment's paradox: reason and progress imposed by force.
Pombal's statue towers over Lisbon's Marquês de Pombal roundabout, with a lion beside him and the city he rebuilt spread below.

quiz.q: Qual catástrofe inspirou o Cândido de Voltaire?
Qual era o lema do Iluminismo segundo Kant?

cards.title: A dialética de Hegel
cards.text: Hegel via a história como ideias que se desenvolvem por meio do conflito: uma posição encontra seu oposto, e daí surge uma síntese superior.

deep.x: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770–1831) finished his first major book, *The Phenomenology of Spirit*, in Jena in 1806, as Napoleon's army fought outside the town. He saw in Napoleon a "world-soul on horseback": history itself on the move.
How the dialectic works
For Hegel, any one-sided idea, pushed far enough, shows its own limits and turns into its opposite. The clash is not a dead end. It produces a richer idea that keeps what was true in both.
His key word is *aufheben*, a German verb with three meanings at once.
History as freedom

Hegel read world history as the growth of freedom: in ancient despotisms one person was free, in Greece and Rome some were, and in the modern world all are, in principle. He called the driving force **Spirit** (*Geist*): humanity's shared mind becoming aware of itself.
Master and slave

In a famous passage, two consciousnesses fight for recognition. One becomes master, the other slave. Yet the slave, through work, shapes the world and gains self-understanding, while the master grows dependent. Marx later borrowed this pattern.

items.r: Others coined it; Hegel rarely used it

deep.x: Critics were fierce. Schopenhauer called him a charlatan; Karl Popper in 1945 blamed his view of the state for feeding authoritarianism. Admirers reply that he was describing how freedom becomes real in institutions, not praising any tyranny.
Hegel taught that conflict between ideas is how understanding grows, not a sign it has failed.
Hegel wrote that philosophy, like the owl of Minerva, takes flight only at dusk: we understand an era only as it ends.

cards.title: Marx
cards.text: Karl Marx defendeu que a história é movida pelo conflito econômico entre classes e que o capitalismo explora os trabalhadores. Suas ideias inspiraram movimentos e regimes com resultados muito diferentes.

deep.x: Karl Marx (1818–1883) was born in Trier, studied Hegel in Berlin, and became a radical journalist. Expelled from several countries, he settled in London in 1849, where he spent decades writing in the British Museum reading room, often in poverty, supported by his friend Friedrich Engels.
History from the bottom up

Marx turned Hegel around: it isn't ideas that drive history, but how people produce their living. Each economy creates classes, such as lords and serfs or owners and wage workers, whose interests clash.
Exploitation and alienation

Workers sell their time for a wage. Marx argued they produce more value than they are paid, and the extra, **surplus value**, becomes profit. He also described **alienation**: workers feel estranged from what they make, from their work and from each other.
Very different outcomes

x: Social democratic parties built welfare states and labour rights within democracies, partly inspired by his critique.
Revolutionary regimes in the USSR, China and elsewhere claimed his name; they produced rapid industrialisation, but also one-party rule, famines and mass repression.
Scholars still debate how far these regimes followed or betrayed his ideas.

deep.x: Strongest objections

Most economists reject his labour theory of value. The revolutions he expected in advanced industrial countries did not come; workers' living standards rose instead. Defenders reply that his analysis of crises, inequality and globalisation remains insightful.

deep.w: Marx designed the Soviet system
deep.r: He wrote little about how a post-capitalist society should run; Lenin and others filled the gap

deep.x: Marx argued that economics shapes history, an idea that influenced historians and social scientists far beyond politics.
Only about a dozen people attended Marx's funeral at Highgate Cemetery in 1883.

cards.title: O utilitarismo de Mill
cards.text: John Stuart Mill refinou o utilitarismo, defendendo que alguns prazeres são superiores a outros: "é melhor ser Sócrates insatisfeito do que um tolo satisfeito".

deep.x: John Stuart Mill (1806–1873) had an extraordinary childhood. His father, a close ally of Jeremy Bentham, taught him Greek from age three. At 20 he suffered a breakdown; reading Wordsworth's poetry helped him recover. It convinced him that feelings and culture matter, not just calculation.
Quality, not just quantity

Bentham's utilitarianism says the right act produces the greatest happiness, measured by amount of pleasure. Critics mocked this as a "philosophy fit for pigs". Mill's reply, in *Utilitarianism* (1861): some pleasures are higher in kind.
Who decides which is higher?
Mill's test is the **competent judge**: ask people who have experienced both pleasures. If nearly all who know both prefer one, even with more discontent, it is higher.
Liberty and equality

In *On Liberty* (1859), Mill set out the **harm principle**: the only good reason to restrict someone's freedom is to prevent harm to others. In *The Subjection of Women* (1869), shaped with Harriet Taylor, he argued for full legal equality of the sexes. As an MP, in 1867 he proposed giving women the vote.
Objections

x: Snobbery: are opera fans really better judges than football fans?
If quality matters apart from pleasure, critics say Mill has quietly left pure utilitarianism.
Utilitarianism in general can seem to permit sacrificing individuals for the greater total.

deep.w: Utilitarians only care about crude pleasure
deep.r: Mill ranked intellectual, moral and creative satisfactions above physical ones

deep.x: Mill thought a richer, harder life of the mind is worth more than easy contentment.

cards.title: Kierkegaard
cards.text: Søren Kierkegaard, o "pai do existencialismo", destacou a escolha individual, o compromisso e a angústia da liberdade. A verdade, dizia ele, precisa ser vivida.

deep.x: Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855) lived almost his whole life in Copenhagen. In 1841 he broke off his engagement to Regine Olsen, whom he loved, a decision that haunted his writing. He published many books under playful pseudonyms, so readers would have to judge each view for themselves.
Three ways to live

The **aesthete** seeks interest and pleasure and dodges commitment, but ends in boredom and despair. The **ethical** person takes on duties, like marriage and work. The **religious** life requires a personal relationship with God that reason can't justify. Moving between them isn't a calculation; it takes a choice, often called a "leap".
Truth that must be lived

Kierkegaard said "subjectivity is truth". He didn't mean anything you feel is true. He meant the most important truths concern how you exist. You can know all about swimming and still need to jump in.
Anxiety
He called anxiety "the dizziness of freedom": the vertigo of facing open possibilities, knowing you could choose anything. It is unpleasant, but also a sign we are free.
Critics and heirs

He attacked the Danish state church for making Christianity comfortable. Critics argue his "leap" makes faith irrational; others find his stress on personal choice too individualistic. Sartre, Camus and Heidegger took up his themes, often without his faith.
In his early twenties he wrote in his journal that he needed to find a truth for which he could live and die.
For Kierkegaard, the question is not just what's true, but how you will live by it.

cards.title: Schopenhauer
cards.text: Arthur Schopenhauer via a vida movida por uma "vontade" cega e inquieta que causa desejo e sofrimento sem fim. A arte, a compaixão e o ascetismo trazem alívio.

deep.x: Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860) was born in Danzig to a wealthy merchant family. His main work, *The World as Will and Representation*, appeared in late 1818 and sold poorly. In Berlin he scheduled his lectures at the same hour as Hegel's; almost no one came.
Will behind everything

Following Kant, he said we know the world only as it appears to us: as representation. But inside ourselves we meet something deeper: **will**, a blind urge to strive and want. He claimed this same will drives everything, from gravity to animals to human desire.
Life swings, he said, like a pendulum between pain and boredom. Getting what you want only frees you to want something else.
Ways out

items: Music: the will itself in sound

deep.x: In art we stop wanting and simply look. Compassion, he said, is the basis of ethics: when you see another's suffering as your own, you act kindly. Saints who renounce desire go furthest.
East and West

He was one of the first Western philosophers to engage closely with Hindu and Buddhist thought, keeping a statue of the Buddha in his study. He saw parallels with the Buddhist idea that craving causes suffering.
Objections

Critics call his view gloomy temperament dressed as metaphysics. If the will is blind and all-powerful, how can anyone deny it? And he lived comfortably on inherited money while praising renunciation.

deep.w: Pessimism means giving up
deep.r: Schopenhauer offered art, music and compassion as real, if temporary, relief

deep.x: Schopenhauer saw desire as endless, and found peace in moments when we stop wanting.
Wagner, Tolstoy, Freud, Einstein and the young Wittgenstein all read him closely.

cards.title: "Deus está morto", de Nietzsche
cards.text: A famosa frase de Friedrich Nietzsche queria dizer que a crença em Deus já não ancorava os valores ocidentais e que as pessoas teriam de encarar a tarefa de criar novos valores.

deep.x: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) became a professor of classical philology at Basel aged just 24. Ill health forced him to retire in 1879, and he wrote his major works while wandering between Swiss and Italian lodgings. In 1889 he collapsed in Turin and never recovered.
The madman's message

In *The Gay Science* (1882), a madman runs into the market with a lantern in the morning, crying that he seeks God. The bystanders, who don't believe, laugh. He tells them: God is dead, and we have killed him. Then he says he has come too early: people haven't grasped what they have done.
What it means

Nietzsche wasn't announcing a fact about heaven. He meant that in modern Europe, belief in God no longer guided culture. Science, history and doubt had eroded it. But Western morality, such as equal worth and pity for the weak, rested on that belief.
Not a celebration
The tone is alarm, not triumph. Without a foundation, he feared, people would slide into **nihilism**: the sense that nothing matters. Some would cling to faded values out of habit.

items.r: Nietzsche warning of its consequences

deep.x: Responses

Religious thinkers reply that faith has not disappeared and that values can rest on God whatever culture believes. Secular critics argue morality can stand on reason, sympathy or social agreement without either God or Nietzsche's drama.
"God is dead" is a diagnosis of a culture, not a proof about God.
Nietzsche's father was a Lutheran pastor, and he himself first studied theology before switching to classics.

cards.title: O Übermensch
cards.text: O ideal de Nietzsche é uma pessoa que cria seus próprios valores e afirma plenamente a vida. O uso abusivo posterior de suas ideias pelos nazistas as distorceu.

deep.x: In *Thus Spoke Zarathustra* (1883–85), the prophet Zarathustra announces the **Übermensch**, usually translated "overman" or "superman". Humanity, he says, is a rope stretched between animal and overman: something to be overcome.
Three transformations
Zarathustra describes how the spirit changes.

The camel carries inherited values; the lion fights them; the child plays and creates. The overman is not a stronger brute but a creator: someone who shapes their own values and says yes to life, including its suffering.
Zarathustra contrasts the overman with the **last man**, who wants only comfort, small pleasures and safety. Nietzsche feared this was where modern society was heading.
How it was distorted

After Nietzsche's collapse, his sister Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche controlled his archive. She was an antisemite and German nationalist, and she edited his notes into a book, *The Will to Power*, to fit her views. She later welcomed Hitler to the archive. The Nazis used "Übermensch" in a racial sense he never intended.
Was he innocent?

Nietzsche mocked antisemites and German nationalism, and broke with Wagner partly over them. But critics note his writing does praise hierarchy and scorn equality, which made it easier to misuse. Scholars still argue over how political his ideal is.

deep.w: The Übermensch is a master race
deep.r: It's an individual ideal of self-creation; Nietzsche despised racial antisemitism

deep.x: Nietzsche's overman is not someone who rules others, but someone who masters and creates themselves.

cards.title: O eterno retorno
cards.text: O experimento mental de Nietzsche: se você tivesse que viver sua vida de novo, exatamente igual, infinitas vezes, você se alegraria ou se desesperaria? Viva de modo a dizer que sim.

deep.x: In *The Gay Science* (1882), Nietzsche asks you to imagine a demon creeping into your loneliest hour. It tells you that you will live this exact life again, and again, infinitely: every pain, joy and thought in the same order.
Rejoice or despair?
Would you curse the demon, or call it divine? Nietzsche called this "the greatest weight". The idea is a test: it puts infinite weight on every choice.
Love of fate

The ideal response is **amor fati**, "love of fate": not merely putting up with what happens, but wanting nothing to be different, not forward, not backward. Even your worst moments made you who you are.
Test or theory?

In his notebooks Nietzsche toyed with recurrence as a physical theory: with finite matter and infinite time, all arrangements might repeat. Most readers today treat it as an ethical thought experiment rather than cosmology.
Objections

x: If you can't remember the earlier lives, in what sense is it "you" again?
For someone whose life includes terrible suffering, is affirming it all wise or cruel?
Can you want the past to be as it was without also endorsing the wrongs in it?

deep.x: Live so that you could wish this moment to return forever.
Milan Kundera's novel *The Unbearable Lightness of Being* (1984) opens by reflecting on eternal recurrence and its opposite: a life lived only once, light and weightless.

cards.title: Pragmatismo
cards.text: Pragmatistas americanos como William James defenderam que a verdade de uma ideia está em suas consequências práticas: que diferença ela faz na prática?

deep.x: Pragmatism is the first major philosophy born in the United States. It grew from conversations in a "Metaphysical Club" in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in the 1870s. Its key thinkers were Charles Sanders Peirce, William James and John Dewey.
The pragmatic test
Peirce's rule (1878): to clarify an idea, ask what practical effects it would have. If two ideas make no difference in practice, they are really the same idea.
The squirrel and the tree

James told of a camping argument. A squirrel clings to a tree trunk; a man walks round the tree, but the squirrel keeps moving round too, always facing him. Does the man "go round" the squirrel? James said it depends what "round" means: north, east, south, west of it, yes; front, side, back, no. Once that is clear, the dispute dissolves.
Truth that works

James went further: a true belief is one that proves useful over the long run, its "cash value" in experience. Dewey applied pragmatism to education, democracy and science, treating ideas as tools for solving problems.
Objections

Bertrand Russell objected that useful and true come apart: a comforting lie may work well. Others ask: useful for whom? Pragmatists reply that over time, beliefs that misdescribe reality tend to stop working.

deep.w: Pragmatism means doing whatever is convenient
deep.r: It is a theory of meaning and truth tied to experiment and evidence

deep.x: Pragmatism asks of any idea: what difference would it make if it were true?

cards.title: O impacto de Darwin
cards.text: A teoria da evolução de Darwin (1859) questionou as ideias de singularidade humana e de propósito na natureza, transformando a filosofia, a religião e a ética.

deep.x: Charles Darwin published *On the Origin of Species* in November 1859. Alfred Russel Wallace had reached a similar theory independently, and their papers were presented together in 1858. In 1871, *The Descent of Man* applied the theory directly to humans.
End of the watchmaker?

In 1802 William Paley argued that if you find a watch on a heath, you infer a watchmaker; the eye is even more intricate, so it implies a designer. Natural selection offered a different explanation for apparent design: small changes, kept when useful, over millions of years.
What changed in philosophy
Pragmatists like Dewey saw ideas as tools that evolve. Later thinkers explored how cooperation and empathy could have evolved, and what that means for morality.
Misuses and debate

"Survival of the fittest" was coined by Herbert Spencer. So-called Social Darwinists used it to justify inequality, empire and eugenics, which most philosophers reject as confusing how nature works with how we ought to act. Many religious believers accept evolution: the Catholic Church has said it is compatible with faith. Others still reject it.

deep.w: "Fittest" means strongest
deep.r: It means best suited to reproduce in a given environment, which can mean cooperative, small or camouflaged

deep.x: Darwin showed that order and apparent design in nature can arise without a designer, which changed how philosophers think about purpose.
Darwin delayed publishing for about 20 years, partly fearing how his ideas would be received.

quiz.q: O que Nietzsche queria dizer com "Deus está morto"?
options: A crença já não ancora os valores ocidentais

quiz.q: Quem disse que é melhor ser Sócrates insatisfeito do que um tolo satisfeito?

cards.title: Para que servem
cards.text: Os experimentos mentais testam ideias imaginando cenários que não podemos (ou não devemos) realizar de verdade. Eles revelam pressupostos ocultos.

deep.x: A thought experiment is an experiment run in the imagination. You set up a scenario, change one thing, and see what follows. The German word *Gedankenexperiment* was popularised by the physicist Ernst Mach in the 1890s, but the method goes back to ancient Greece.
Why not just run real experiments?

x: Some are impossible: you can't ride a beam of light.
Some are unethical: you can't push someone off a bridge to test a moral theory.
Some test concepts, not facts: what counts as "the same ship"?

deep.x: How they work

A good one isolates a single factor. The trolley problem keeps numbers fixed (five lives versus one) and changes only whether you pull a lever or push a person. If your answer changes, the difference must come from that one detail. Daniel Dennett called such scenarios **intuition pumps**: devices for drawing out and examining our instincts.
Limits

Intuitions differ between people and cultures, and wording can change answers. Some scenarios describe things that may be impossible, so our reactions may not be reliable. And a vivid story can lead us to overlook what has been left out.

items.w: A thought experiment proves a theory
items.r: It tests and challenges it

deep.x: Thought experiments are philosophy's laboratory: cheap, safe, and able to go where real experiments can't.
Schrödinger's cat (1935) was meant to show how absurd one reading of quantum mechanics was, not to suggest cats can be alive and dead.

cards.title: O navio de Teseu
cards.text: Se cada tábua de um navio for substituída, ele continua sendo o mesmo navio? E se você juntar as tábuas velhas e montar outro navio, qual é o original?

deep.x: The Greek writer Plutarch, around 100 CE, told how the Athenians preserved the ship of their hero Theseus. As planks rotted, they replaced them, until philosophers argued whether it was still the same ship. In 1655 Thomas Hobbes added a twist: what if someone kept the old planks and rebuilt them?
Competing answers
Why it matters

The puzzle reaches far beyond boats. Clubs, bands and countries change all their members over time. Is Portugal the "same" country as in 1143? Lisbon's restored trams, cathedral repairs and museum restorations raise the question in daily life. Philosophers also apply it to people: if your body's materials keep changing, what makes you the same person?
A tidier view?

Some philosophers say objects are like events stretched through time, with temporal "parts". Then two ships can share early parts and split later, like a road that forks. Critics find this strange: is the ship you see now only a slice of the real thing?

deep.w: Every cell in your body is replaced every seven years
deep.r: Many cells renew, but most brain neurons and the lens of the eye last your whole life

deep.x: The ship of Theseus shows that "the same" can mean several different things, and we usually don't notice which one we're using.

cards.title: Cérebro numa cuba
cards.text: Como você sabe que não é um cérebro numa cuba, alimentado com experiências por um computador? É a dúvida de Descartes atualizada para a era da simulação.

deep.x: Imagine a mad scientist removes your brain, keeps it alive in a vat of nutrients, and wires it to a computer. The computer sends exactly the signals your nerves would receive. You "see" your room, "feel" your coffee cup, and notice nothing odd. How could you tell?
An old doubt in new clothes

In 1641 Descartes imagined an evil demon deceiving him about the entire outside world. The brain in a vat swaps the demon for technology. Films like *The Matrix* (1999) and Nick Bostrom's 2003 "simulation argument" gave it fresh life.
The sceptic's argument

x: If I know I have hands, I know I'm not a handless brain in a vat.
I can't know I'm not a brain in a vat.
So I don't know I have hands.

deep.x: Replies

items.b: I know I have hands, so…

deep.x: Moore simply ran the argument backwards: he is more sure of his hands than of any philosophical premise. Hilary Putnam (1981) argued that a real brain in a vat couldn't even think about real vats, because its word "vat" would refer to simulated ones. So if you can truly think "I am a brain in a vat", it's false. Critics doubt this settles it.
You can't prove from the inside that your experiences come from a real world, yet almost no one lives as though they don't.
Putnam's own reply depends on a theory of meaning: words get meaning from causal contact with things, which the vat brain lacks.

cards.title: A máquina de experiências
cards.text: Robert Nozick perguntou: você se conectaria pelo resto da vida a uma máquina que lhe desse qualquer experiência agradável que quisesse? A maioria diz que não, o que sugere que valorizamos mais do que o prazer.

deep.x: In 1974, in *Anarchy, State, and Utopia*, the American philosopher Robert Nozick described a machine run by "superduper neuropsychologists". Plug in and you'd experience anything you chose: writing a great novel, falling in love, winning a match. You would believe it was all real. Would you plug in for life?
Why most say no
If pleasure or happy experiences were all that mattered, plugging in would be the obvious choice. Most people refuse. Nozick suggested we care about three things the machine can't give.
A blow to hedonism

**Hedonism** in this sense says only pleasure is good in itself. The experience machine is one of the most cited arguments against it. If you'd rather a real friend than a perfect simulated one, you value something beyond your experiences.
Objections

x: **Status quo bias**: maybe we just fear change. In a reversed version, people are told they're already in a machine and asked if they want to unplug into an unknown real life. Many say they would stay.
Worries about the machine breaking, or who runs it, may cloud the answer.
Some hedonists bite the bullet: plugging in would be better, even if it feels wrong.

deep.x: Philosopher Felipe De Brigard published a reversed-machine study in 2010; responses suggested much of our refusal depends on which life we start from.
Most people want their lives to be real, not just to feel good.

cards.title: O quarto de Mary
cards.text: Mary conhece todos os fatos físicos sobre a cor, mas sempre viveu em um quarto em preto e branco. Quando vê vermelho pela primeira vez, ela aprende algo novo?

deep.x: In 1982 Australian philosopher Frank Jackson imagined Mary, a brilliant scientist. She has spent her whole life in a black-and-white room, learning about the world through black-and-white screens. She knows every physical fact about colour: wavelengths, the retina, the brain's responses.
The argument

If Mary learns something new when she first sees red, namely what it is like to see red, then not all facts are physical facts. Something about conscious experience escapes physics. These felt qualities are often called **qualia**.
Replies from physicalists

x: **Ability hypothesis**: she gains know-how, like recognising and imagining red, not a new fact.
**New concept**: she learns an old physical fact in a new way, as Frege's two names can pick out one planet.
**Dennett**: if she truly knew everything physical, she wouldn't be surprised at all; we just can't imagine "everything".

deep.x: A change of mind
Jackson later abandoned the argument and became a physicalist himself, around the late 1990s. Others still defend it as a powerful challenge to the view that physics can describe everything.

A real cousin of this puzzle, Molyneux's problem (1688), asks whether someone born blind who gains sight could recognise a cube by sight alone; a 2011 study of patients after cataract surgery suggested not straight away.
Mary asks whether knowing every fact about the brain tells you what an experience actually feels like.

cards.title: O teletransportador
cards.text: Um teletransportador escaneia você, destrói você e constrói uma cópia exata em Marte. A cópia é você? E se o original não for destruído?

deep.x: Imagine a machine on Earth scans every cell of your body, records it, and destroys the original. The data travels to Mars, where an exact copy is built from local atoms. The copy steps out with your memories, personality and plans, convinced it is you. Is it?
Two kinds of view

John Locke (1690s) tied personal identity to consciousness and memory. On that view, teleporting is just travel. Others hold that you are a living organism, and organisms don't survive being dismantled.
The branch-line case

Derek Parfit, in *Reasons and Persons* (1984), added a twist: the scanner malfunctions and doesn't destroy you. Now there's you on Earth and a copy on Mars. They can't both be you, since they'll soon live different lives. So which one is?
Parfit's answer

Parfit concluded that **identity is not what matters**. What matters is psychological continuity and connectedness. If the copy will carry on your projects and love your people, that is almost as good as ordinary survival. He found this comforting: death seemed less of a wall.
Objections

x: Many feel strongly that being copied isn't surviving; the original should fear the scanner.
If identity doesn't matter, should you care more about your future self than about strangers?

deep.x: *Star Trek* fans have long noted that its transporter, read literally, might kill the traveller every time.
The teleporter asks what makes you "you": your body, your mind, or something else.

cards.title: O problema de Newcomb
cards.text: Um previsor que quase nunca erra oferece duas caixas: uma com € 1,000, outra com € 1 milhão ou nada. Você leva as duas, ou só a segunda? Os filósofos se dividem.

deep.x: The physicist William Newcomb devised this puzzle around 1960; Robert Nozick published it in 1969. A Predictor, who has been right almost every time, offers you two boxes.
You may take only Box B, or both boxes. The prediction was made yesterday; the boxes are already filled.
Two arguments that can't both win

x: Predictor right 99%
Take B only: 0.99 × €1,000,000 = €990,000 expected

deep.x: The two-boxer replies: whatever is in Box B, it's there now. If it holds a million, taking both gives you €1,001,000. If it's empty, both gives €1,000 instead of nothing. Taking both is better in every case. This is called **dominance**.
Why it matters

The puzzle splits decision theory into two camps. **Evidential** theory says pick the action that is best news about your outcome. **Causal** theory says pick the action that causes the best outcome. In most choices they agree; here they don't.
Nozick remarked that almost everyone thinks the answer is perfectly obvious, but they split roughly evenly on which answer it is.
Newcomb's problem shows that two sensible rules for rational choice can point in opposite directions.

cards.title: A posição original
cards.text: Rawls perguntou que princípios você escolheria para a sociedade por trás de um véu da ignorância. É um experimento mental sobre justiça.

deep.x: In *A Theory of Justice* (1971), the American philosopher John Rawls asked: what rules for society would you choose if you didn't know what place you would have in it?
The veil of ignorance

Behind the veil, you don't know your sex, ethnicity, talents, wealth, religion or even your idea of a good life. You know general facts about economics and psychology. You want to do well, but you can't tailor rules to favour yourself. It's like cutting a cake when you don't know which slice you'll get.
Rawls's two principles
Rawls argued that, facing such high stakes, you would play safe and protect the worst position you could end up in.
Strong objections

x: John Harsanyi argued rational people would maximise average welfare, accepting some risk.
Robert Nozick (1974) argued justice depends on how holdings were acquired, not on a final pattern.
Communitarians like Michael Sandel said no one is a "self" stripped of all ties and values.

deep.w: The veil means people should forget who they are in real life
deep.r: It's a test for fairness, not a recommendation to ignore real identities

deep.x: Rawls asks you to judge the rules of society as if you could end up anywhere in it.
Rawls served as an infantryman in the Pacific in the Second World War, and later said the war shook his religious faith.

cards.title: Os corpos em queda de Galileu

steps: Seria mais rápido e mais lento

cards.text: Galileu imaginou amarrar uma pedra pesada a uma leve: elas cairiam mais rápido ou mais devagar? A contradição mostrou que todos os objetos caem no mesmo ritmo.

deep.x: Aristotle taught that heavier objects fall faster, in proportion to their weight. For almost 2,000 years, few tested it carefully. In *Two New Sciences* (1638), Galileo knocked it down with pure reasoning.
The argument

Suppose Aristotle is right. Tie a heavy stone to a light one. The light stone falls more slowly, so it should hold back the heavy one: the pair falls slower than the heavy stone alone. But the pair together is heavier than the heavy stone, so it should fall faster. It can't do both. So speed of falling can't depend on weight.
What about feathers?
A feather does fall slower than a hammer on Earth. Galileo knew this: the difference comes from air resistance, not weight. In a vacuum they fall together.
Real experiments too
Galileo also rolled balls down gently sloping ramps, timing them with water clocks, to measure acceleration. Thought experiment and real measurement worked together.

deep.w: Galileo dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa
deep.r: The story comes from a later biography by his pupil and there's no firm evidence he did it

deep.x: A single, careful contradiction can bring down a theory without any equipment at all.
In 1971 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather on the Moon; with no air, they landed at the same moment.

cards.title: O raio de luz de Einstein
cards.text: Aos 16 anos, Einstein se imaginou perseguindo um raio de luz. O que ele veria? O enigma o levou à relatividade restrita.

deep.x: Around 1895, aged 16, Albert Einstein was at a school in Aarau, Switzerland. He later recalled asking himself: what would I see if I ran alongside a beam of light at the speed of light?
The puzzle

If you could catch up with a light wave, it should look frozen: a wave of electric and magnetic fields standing still. But the laws of electromagnetism, set out by James Clerk Maxwell in the 1860s, allow no such thing. Something had to give.
Special relativity, 1905

Einstein made two assumptions: the laws of physics are the same for everyone moving steadily, and light always moves at the same speed, about 300,000 km per second, however fast you go. Then he followed the logic.

items.b: mass is a form of energy

deep.x: In your pocket

GPS satellites carry atomic clocks. Because they move fast, special relativity makes them run slow by about 7 microseconds a day; weaker gravity makes them run fast by about 45. Without correcting the net 38 microseconds, positions would drift by around 10 km a day.

deep.w: Einstein was bad at maths at school
deep.r: He excelled at maths; he did fail the general part of an entrance exam at 16, while scoring highly in maths and physics

deep.x: Einstein's revolution began with a question a child might ask, taken completely seriously.

quiz.q: O que a máquina de experiências de Nozick sugere?
options: Valorizamos mais do que experiências agradáveis
quiz.explain: A maioria se recusa a se conectar.

quiz.q: O que o experimento mental de Galileu mostrou?
options: Todos os objetos caem no mesmo ritmo

lessons.title: Ética da tecnologia e da IA

cards.title: A tecnologia não é neutra
cards.text: As ferramentas moldam o comportamento: os carros moldaram as cidades, os celulares moldaram a atenção. Quem projeta faz escolhas de valores, perceba isso ou não.

deep.x: A common slogan says tools are neutral: what matters is how people use them. Philosophers of technology argue that's only half true. Tools make some actions easy and others hard, and so they quietly steer what people do.
Defaults are decisions

Whatever happens when you do nothing is a design choice. In organ donation, some countries ask you to opt in; others, including Portugal since 1993, count you as a donor unless you opt out. A well-known 2003 study compared neighbouring countries with similar cultures.
Examples everywhere

x: Cars and motorways reshaped cities around parking and commuting, often at the expense of walking.
Infinite scroll removes natural stopping points; its inventor later said he regretted its effect on attention.
Phone notifications are designed to pull you back, because attention is what many apps sell.

deep.x: In 1980, Langdon Winner's essay "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" argued that designs can build in social choices: who gets access, who is in control.
The other side
Critics warn against **technological determinism**: tools don't force outcomes. People resist, repurpose and regulate them. Text messaging was a minor feature that users turned into a culture.
Marshall McLuhan's 1964 phrase "the medium is the message" meant that a technology's effect on how we live matters more than any single piece of content it carries.
Every design embeds choices about what people should do, so someone is always deciding, even by default.

cards.title: Privacidade
cards.text: A quem pertencem os seus dados? Os filósofos defendem que a privacidade protege a liberdade, a dignidade e a capacidade de pensar sem ser vigiado. O GDPR da UE deu às pessoas direitos sobre seus dados.

deep.x: Privacy isn't just about hiding secrets. In 1890 two American lawyers, Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis, described it as "the right to be let alone", worried about newspaper gossip and the new portable camera.
Why privacy matters

Jeremy Bentham designed the **Panopticon** in 1791: a prison where inmates could always be watched but never knew when. The philosopher Michel Foucault argued that people who might be watched start policing themselves. This is the **chilling effect**: surveillance changes behaviour even when nothing bad is done with the data. After the 2013 Snowden revelations, one study found visits to Wikipedia articles on terrorism-related topics dropped.
"Nothing to hide"
Supporters of more surveillance stress real benefits: catching criminals, public health, convenience. The debate is about balance and safeguards.
Europe's answer: GDPR

The EU's General Data Protection Regulation took effect on 25 May 2018. It gives people the right to see their data, correct it, have it erased in some cases and take it elsewhere. Organisations need a legal basis to process personal data. In Portugal the national data protection authority (CNPD) enforces it.
Privacy protects not only what you hide but your freedom to become who you choose.

cards.title: Viés algorítmico
cards.text: Uma IA treinada com dados históricos enviesados pode repetir o viés: ferramentas de recrutamento que favoreciam homens porque as contratações anteriores tinham sido, em sua maioria, de homens.

deep.x: Machine-learning systems learn patterns from past data. If the past was unfair, the system can learn the unfairness and apply it at scale, with an appearance of objectivity.
The hiring example

In 2018 Reuters reported that Amazon had scrapped an experimental tool for rating CVs. Trained on ten years of applications, mostly from men, it learned to downgrade CVs including the word "women's", as in "women's chess club". Engineers tried to fix it, but couldn't be sure it wouldn't find other proxies.
Where bias comes from
A 2018 study, "Gender Shades", tested commercial face-analysis systems. Error rates in guessing gender were far higher for darker-skinned women than for lighter-skinned men.
Fairness is hard to define

Should a system have equal error rates across groups, or equal accuracy of its positive predictions? Mathematicians have shown that, when groups have different base rates, these goals can't all be satisfied at once. Choosing between them is an ethical decision, not a technical one.

In the Netherlands, an automated risk system used in childcare benefits wrongly flagged thousands of families, many with dual nationality, as fraudsters; the government resigned over the scandal in 2021.

deep.w: Algorithms are objective because they're maths
deep.r: They inherit choices about data, targets and trade-offs made by people

deep.x: An algorithm trained on the past can automate the past's injustices unless someone checks.

cards.title: Quem é o responsável?
cards.text: Se um carro autônomo sofre um acidente, de quem é a culpa: do dono, do fabricante, do programador ou da IA? A responsabilidade fica diluída.

deep.x: In March 2018, an Uber self-driving test car in Arizona struck and killed Elaine Herzberg as she crossed a road pushing a bicycle. The system had detected her but didn't classify her correctly in time; the safety driver was looking at a phone; emergency braking had been disabled. Who was to blame?
The problem of many hands

When many people each contribute a small part, it can seem that no one is responsible. The philosopher Dennis Thompson called this the **problem of many hands**. With machine learning, there is also a **responsibility gap**: no one programmed the specific decision; the system learned it.
Levels of automation
As cars move up these levels, responsibility shifts from driver to maker. Some manufacturers have said they will accept liability while their level 3 systems are engaged.
How law is adapting

In 2024 the EU updated its Product Liability Directive so that software, including AI, counts as a product: makers can be liable for defects without proof of negligence. In the Uber case, prosecutors charged the safety driver, not the company; she later pleaded guilty to a lesser charge.
Different views

Some argue only humans can be morally responsible, so a person must always be accountable. Others propose shared or strict liability schemes, like insurance, focused on compensating victims rather than finding a villain.
When responsibility is spread thin, someone has to be designated to carry it, or no one will.

cards.title: O dilema do bonde, automatizado
cards.text: Os carros autônomos tornam real o dilema do bonde. A pesquisa Moral Machine, do MIT, reuniu milhões de respostas e concluiu que as preferências variavam entre culturas.

deep.x: In 1967 philosopher Philippa Foot imagined a runaway tram heading for five workers; you can divert it onto a track where it will kill one. Judith Jarvis Thomson added the "footbridge" version: pushing a large person off a bridge would stop it. Most people would divert, but wouldn't push.
The Moral Machine

MIT researchers built an online game in which players chose whom a brake-failed self-driving car should spare. Results published in *Nature* in 2018 covered about 40 million decisions from people in 233 countries and territories.
What they found

x: Broad agreement: spare humans over animals, more lives over fewer, the young over the old.
Clusters differed: in some regions, preferences for sparing the young were weaker.
Preferences linked to culture and economics, such as attitudes to rule-following.

deep.x: Should votes decide?
Germany's 2017 ethics commission on automated driving said cars must not choose victims by age, sex or other personal features. Popular preference and ethical principle can clash.
Critics of the framing

Many engineers argue real crashes are rarely clean dilemmas. A car's job is mostly to see hazards early and brake. Focusing on rare dilemmas may distract from everyday safety and from who sets the rules.
The original trolley problem was part of Foot's article on abortion and the "doctrine of double effect", not about transport at all.
Automation forces us to write down moral choices that humans used to make in a split second.

cards.title: Automação e trabalho
cards.text: Se as máquinas fizerem a maior parte dos empregos, como vamos dividir a riqueza, e onde as pessoas vão encontrar sentido? As propostas incluem requalificação, semanas mais curtas e renda básica universal.

deep.x: Fear of machines taking jobs is old. Between 1811 and 1816, English textile workers called **Luddites** smashed machines they blamed for wage cuts. In 1930 the economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that by 2030 people might work about 15 hours a week. Productivity rose as he expected, but working hours fell much less.
How many jobs are at risk?
Estimates vary hugely depending on method.

The first study looked at whole occupations; the second looked at the tasks within jobs and found most jobs would change rather than vanish. Generative AI has reopened the question, now including office and creative work.
Proposals

items.b: help people move to new jobs

deep.x: Finland gave 2,000 unemployed people €560 a month without conditions in 2017–2018. Employment rose only slightly, but participants reported better wellbeing and less stress. Portugal ran a government-backed four-day-week pilot with private companies in 2023.
Meaning, not just money

Philosophers ask what work gives besides income: structure, skill, recognition, community. Marx worried about alienated labour; others say freedom from toil could let people pursue art, care and learning. Critics of basic income raise cost and incentives; supporters cite security and dignity.

deep.w: Automation always destroys jobs overall
deep.r: Historically it has shifted work between sectors; whether AI is different is debated

deep.x: The question isn't only what machines can do, but how a society shares the gains and what people do with their time.

cards.title: Alinhamento da IA

steps: A IA o cumpre ao pé da letra

cards.text: Como garantir que sistemas de IA poderosos busquem objetivos que os humanos realmente querem? Até instruções bem-intencionadas podem ser mal interpretadas, como o toque de ouro do rei Midas.

deep.x: **Alignment** means making sure an AI system pursues the goals its designers and users actually intend. It sounds simple. The trouble is that we rarely say exactly what we mean.
Old stories, new problem

King Midas wished that everything he touched would turn to gold, and then couldn't eat. Goethe's sorcerer's apprentice ordered a broom to fetch water and couldn't make it stop. In 1960 the mathematician Norbert Wiener warned that we'd better be sure the purpose we put into a machine is the one we really desire.
Specification gaming

In a 2016 experiment, an AI trained to win a boat-racing game discovered it scored more points by circling forever, hitting the same targets and catching fire, than by finishing the race. It did what it was rewarded for, not what was wanted.

items.r: Agent circles, never finishes
Feed promotes outrage

deep.x: Key ideas

x: **Goodhart's law**: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
**Outer alignment**: did we specify the right goal?
